bio.en: Anuj Rathi is Chief Product and Marketing Officer at Jupiter Money, previously SVP of Revenue and Growth at Swiggy, VP of Product at Snapdeal, and the first PM at Flipkart's buyer experience team.
bio.zh: Anuj Rathi 是 Jupiter Money 首席产品与营销官，此前曾任 Swiggy 营收与增长高级副总裁、Snapdeal 产品副总裁，以及 Flipkart 买家体验团队的第一位产品经理。

summary.en: Anuj explains how product management differs in India and shares lessons on building product experiences for new-to-internet users at massive scale. He describes operationalizing Amazon's “working backwards” process and why he pushes teams to explore three divergent directions before settling on a plan. The conversation also covers why PMs and companies should be far more full-stack than they typically are.
summary.zh: Anuj 解释了印度市场的产品管理有何不同，并分享了为海量“新上网用户”打造产品体验的心得。他讲述了如何将亚马逊的“逆向工作法”落地，以及为何他推动团队在定案前先探索三个截然不同的方向。对话还涵盖为何产品经理和公司应当比现在更“全栈”。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: There are only three reasons why things do not happen the way you want them to happen as a leader. You can look at a person, and you would say either that person can't do, which is a capability issue, or they won't do, which is a motivation or an alignment issue, or they were not set up to do, which is really your problem that you didn't set up the ways of working now design properly. So, as a leader, do you have the right people in terms of capability? If not, is the right answer for us to coach them or to really put them... or mentor them and so on, or move them to some other place because maybe their capability is suited elsewhere? If they won't do, why won't they? Are they not aligned to you? Do they not agree with your vision? Do they not just have enough time? So on and so forth. So you need to really go deeper there. Why won't they do?
turns.zh: 作为领导者，事情没有按照你希望的方式发生的原因只有三个。你可以看着一个人，你会说这个人要么做不到，这是一个能力问题，要么他们不会做，这是一个动机或一致性问题，或者他们没有被设置去做，这实际上是你的问题，你没有正确设置现在设计的工作方式。那么，作为领导者，你是否拥有合适的人才？如果不是，那么正确的答案是我们指导他们或真正安置他们......或指导他们等等，或者将他们转移到其他地方，因为也许他们的能力适合其他地方？如果他们不做，为什么不做？他们与你不一致吗？他们不同意你的愿景吗？他们的时间还不够吗？等等。所以你需要真正深入那里。他们为什么不这样做？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You're very modest. I wanted to start with a question about product in India, and I'm just curious just how is product management and product building in general just most different in India?
turns.zh: 惊人的。你很谦虚。我想从一个关于印度产品的问题开始，我只是很好奇印度的产品管理和产品构建总体上有何不同？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's a very interesting question, and I think about this all the time. When I look at product management in India, and I do have a lot of friends comparing product management versus in US or even in Europe versus even in China, Southeast Asia, et cetera. I think India has had a very interesting journey of products in general and hence, product management also. I think till about 2010-ish, there were not really many products built for the Indian consumers in the first place. There were a lot of products being built, a lot of technology being built, but largely, because it was a back office, so you had a lot of great engineers working in companies which would build products for the American customer or even for the European customer and so on. So once these startups started coming in, which were thinking about building for the Indian consumers, I think we did not really have that talent which we could directly tap into. We're trained into product building. Forget product management as a field in the first place. There were no colleges which were teaching anything about this. There was no playbooks, and so on, and so forth. We would go to the internet, and look at YouTube, and look at SVPG and all of that, but what we would understand would not... you could not put directly to the Indian startups. (00:06:48): The way that they shaped up I think also shaped up the way product management field would evolve in India. So it's taken a bunch of iterations, and I think there are two or three different waves that have come in, and we are way closer to how good product management should be done in India. We still have a little bit way to go compared to, say, US. I also think of it along... For example, in US, the product building culture probably started in 1970s, the modern software product building culture, and you didn't only have product manager, but the entire ecosystem... If you think about a company, who is the VP of business, and who is the VP of supply, and sales, and ops, and technology, and all of that? That group knew how to work with each other to build software products. They understood how that would be built and what to expect. (00:07:37): I think in India, when we were in 2010, et cetera, even those different people who needed to come together to build, say, e-commerce, they would come from, say, FMCG, or they would come from manufacturing and so on. What they would have seen in their journeys in terms of what we expect is a very request response kind of understanding which is, "Here's machinery. If I give this X resources, I expect, with a little bit of variability, why predictable output will come," and that mentality also moved on to what I expect from product managers or product building journeys and so on. So I think over a period of time, a lot of those cycles have happened, and a lot more other leaders in companies have now seen those cycles and understood, "All right. Now, I understand software is not machinery. Consumers are not predictable as much as we thought." That has led to, now, finally, I think, product management coming of age.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这是一个非常有趣的问题，我一直在思考这个问题。当我观察印度的产品管理时，我确实有很多朋友将产品管理与美国甚至欧洲的产品管理与中国、东南亚等地的产品管理进行比较。我认为印度的产品之旅总体上非常有趣，因此产品管理也是如此。我认为直到 2010 年左右，一开始并没有太多为印度消费者打造的产品。有很多产品正在构建，很多技术正在构建，但很大程度上，因为它是一个后台办公室，所以你有很多优秀的工程师在为美国客户甚至欧洲客户等构建产品的公司工作。因此，一旦这些初创公司开始进来，考虑为印度消费者打造产品，我认为我们并没有真正拥有可以直接利用的人才。我们接受过产品构建方面的培训。首先忘记产品管理作为一个领域。没有任何大学教授这方面的内容。没有剧本等等。我们会上网，看看 YouTube，看看 SVPG 等等，但我们所理解的不会……你不能直接把它放在印度初创公司身上。 (00:06:48)：我认为他们的形成方式也塑造了印度产品管理领域的发展方式。因此，这经历了一系列的迭代，我认为已经出现了两到三个不同的浪潮，我们离在印度应该如何进行良好的产品管理已经更近了。与美国相比，我们还有一段路要走。我也想到了......例如，在美国，产品构建文化可能始于 1970 年代，现代软件产品构建文化，你不仅有产品经理，还有整个生态系统......如果你想想一家公司，谁是业务副总裁，谁是供应副总裁，销售副总裁，运营副总裁，技术副总裁，以及所有这些？该团队知道如何相互合作来构建软件产品。他们了解如何构建以及期望什么。 (00:07:37)：我认为在印度，当我们在 2010 年等时候，即使是那些需要聚集在一起建立电子商务等不同的人，他们也会来自快速消费品，或者来自制造业等。他们在旅程中看到的就是我们所期望的一种非常请求响应的理解，即“这是机器。如果我提供 X 资源，我期望，有一点可变性，为什么会出现可预测的输出，”这种心态也转移到了我对产品经理或产品构建旅程等的期望。因此，我认为在一段时间内，已经发生了很多这样的周期，并且公司中更多的其他领导者现在已经看到了这些周期并理解了，“好吧。现在，我明白软件不是机器。消费者并不像我们想象的那样可预测。”我认为，这最终导致了产品管理的成熟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that, I guess, in the Bay Area, things started 1970s, something like that. When would you say things started to really ramp up in modern product thinking in India?
turns.zh: 我想，你说过，在湾区，事情始于 20 世纪 70 年代，类似的事情。您认为印度的现代产品思维什么时候开始真正兴起？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: I think 2010 was when it started because... Look, there were a few products that were built before that also, and I think somebody said this clearly that usually, when modern consumer internet starts coming in countries, it usually starts with travel, so you do have... Basically, any country, we would start with, usually, the first travel company. So I think India started with some companies like MakeMyTrip and so on way earlier. There were a few very interesting products being built in India which were solving uniquely for the Indian consumers that were in the matrimony side which is Shaadi.com, and Bharmatrimony.com, and so on. We're like, "What do you think about Tinder?" India is famous for arranged marriages, so a product that would really understand that, "Hey, if you're a parent, if you want to get your kid up for matrimony, how would you solve for them?" and that marketplace of matchmaking, et cetera started. (00:09:34): So a few blips here and there which was following uniquely for India. I think 2010 was a decade or time when I can very clearly imagine that's where a lot of people started building for India. So I think, again, Flipkart started that kind of journey, but in a couple of years, then they were like, say, Ola which was, in a way, similar to Uber, what they were doing elsewhere, and then a whole bunch of other startups that started coming in. So, for example, in food delivery, when I was working at Swiggy, that came in like, say, 2015, 2014, in that timeframe. Now, you see a whole bunch of startups which are trying to do not only things which are... what could an Uber for India look like or what could a DoorDash for India look like. Very different and also, very innovative. So I think now is the time when you see a lot more product building around that area.
turns.zh: 我认为 2010 年是它开始的时候，因为……看，在那之前也有一些产品，我想有人明确表示，通常，当现代消费者互联网开始进入国家时，它通常从旅行开始，所以你确实有……基本上，任何国家，我们通常都会从第一家旅游公司开始。所以我认为印度很早就开始了像 MakeMyTrip 等这样的公司。印度正在开发一些非常有趣的产品，这些产品为婚姻方面的印度消费者提供了独特的解决方案，例如 Shaadi.com 和 Bharmatrimony.com 等。我们会问“你觉得 Tinder 怎么样？”印度以包办婚姻而闻名，因此一款产品能够真正理解“嘿，如果你是父母，如果你想让你的孩子结婚，你会如何解决他们的问题？”婚介市场等也开始了。 (00:09:34)：这里那里出现了一些印度特有的现象。我认为 2010 年是我可以非常清楚地想象到很多人开始为印度建设的十年。所以我认为，Flipkart 再次开始了这样的旅程，但几年后，他们就像 Ola，在某种程度上类似于 Uber，他们在其他地方所做的事情，然后一大堆其他初创公司开始进入。所以，例如，在食品配送领域，当我在 Swiggy 工作时，就像 2015 年、2014 年那样，在那个时间段内出现了。现在，你会看到一大群初创公司不仅试图做一些事情……印度的 Uber 是什么样子，印度的 DoorDash 是什么样子。非常不同，也非常创新。所以我认为现在是时候看到围绕该领域构建更多产品的时候了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where are some numbers of just like companies in India, people in India's money spent in India? I don't know. Things that would be like, "Wow, that is a much bigger opportunity than I thought."
turns.zh: 印度有多少类似的公司，印度人的钱都花在印度了？我不知道。事情就像是，“哇，这比我想象的要大得多。”

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Okay. This is a very wide question, so I'll tell you. Before the opportunity in India, I think I'll talk about the complexity in India which I think a lot of people don't understand. India has what? 1.4 billion people. So there were three waves, really, that happened in India, but also, in the globe. I think first wave was from desktop to mobile, and then even from mobile to smartphones. From smartphones, there was what we call the Jio revolution. There's an Indian company called Reliance Jio that basically got internet at the cheapest prices for smartphones. So because of this, a whole population came onto the internet which was hungry for newer products, newer content, completely different ways of interacting with each other, and using internet for all sorts of different things. That was one of the waves. (00:11:24): The other part is really what the Indian government really enabled which is... especially in digitization of a bunch of absolute core fundamental citizen-related machinery which is either through digital payments, which is a whole bunch of Indians now started having a bank account by default, and something called UPI. So even if you do not have a bank account or that bank account is linked to your mobile phone number, but now everybody would pay through that, and that brought in a very different kind of revolution. So even if 5 rupees, that is basically 10 cents or less than that, that would be paid through UPI, and people started moving away from cash and so on. There's something called the India Stack that is all of these things coming together, which is social security, identity, payments, and so on, that a whole bunch of other apps can now use to build their own layers on top of that. So many interesting cases started coming about. So that's one which is just a number and the infrastructure. (00:12:25): Now, the other thing to look at is India is very diverse, so the number of languages spoken here, even the official languages is so high, and they say... There's an elders' quote in India like, "Every 15 miles, the language will change, and the people and the culture will change, and it's a huge country of so many people." So your traditional ways of thinking about products also, the "Who I'm building for?" is very different. "Are you building for this person or that?" Et cetera. So a bunch of frameworks break down because it's not even that the same language will apply. While English is a language that is used by the people at least who have the money and who have the dollar to even give to you, but you have to think way more widely. (00:13:06): The other thing about India that is interesting is the price that people are willing to pay. Generally, it does look at the per capita money that people have. It is very low. It's in the two, two and a half thousand dollar range compared to US which is maybe 30 times more and so on. So while there's a lot of people who are going to give you traffic, and engagement, and so on, but the craft of actually choosing the right kind of paying customer who will actually come, and engage, and give you money is at a premium. So a lot harder work needs to be done. If you're running e-commerce, who are the people who will pay me delivery fee? Who are the people who will actually buy this expensive stuff? So a whole bunch of different ways of thinking has evolved in this country, and that's why it's so vibrant and so different than any other global products.
turns.zh: 好的。这是一个非常广泛的问题，所以我来告诉你。在印度的机会之前，我想我会谈谈印度的复杂性，我认为很多人不理解这一点。印度有什么？ 14亿人。因此，确实发生了三波浪潮，不仅发生在印度，而且发生在全球。我认为第一波浪潮是从桌面到移动，然后甚至从移动到智能手机。从智能手机开始，出现了我们所说的 Jio 革命。有一家名为 Reliance Jio 的印度公司，基本上以最便宜的智能手机价格接入互联网。正因为如此，整个人群来到了互联网上，他们渴望更新的产品、更新的内容、完全不同的彼此互动方式，以及使用互联网来做各种不同的事情。那是其中一波浪潮。 (00:11:24)：另一部分实际上是印度政府真正启用的，特别是在一堆绝对核心的基本公民相关机制的数字化方面，这些机制要么通过数字支付，要么通过数字支付，现在很多印度人开始默认拥有银行账户，以及称为 UPI 的东西。因此，即使你没有银行账户，或者银行账户与你的手机号码相关联，但现在每个人都可以通过它进行支付，这带来了一场非常不同的革命。因此，即使 5 卢比（基本上是 10 美分或更少），也可以通过 UPI 支付，人们开始放弃现金等。有一种叫做“印度堆栈”的东西，它把所有这些东西聚集在一起，包括社会保障、身份、支付等等，一大堆其他应用程序现在可以使用它来构建自己的层。许多有趣的案例开始出现。所以这只是一个数字和基础设施。 (00:12:25)：现在，另一件事是印度非常多样化，所以这里使用的语言数量，甚至官方语言都非常多，他们说......印度有一句长辈的话，“每 15 英里，语言就会改变，人民和文化也会改变，这是一个人口众多的大国。”所以你对产品的传统思考方式也是如此，即“我为谁打造？”是非常不同的。 “你是为这个人还是那个人建造？”等等。因此，一堆框架崩溃了，因为甚至无法应用相同的语言。虽然英语是一种至少有钱甚至有美元给你的人使用的语言，但你必须更广泛地思考。 (00:13:06)：印度另一件有趣的事情是人们愿意支付的价格。一般来说，它确实着眼于人们的人均拥有的金钱。它非常低。与美国相比，它的价格在两千、两千五千美元之间，可能是美国的 30 倍等等。因此，虽然有很多人会给你带来流量、参与度等等，但真正选择真正会来、参与并给你钱的正确类型的付费客户的技巧是非常宝贵的。因此，还需要做很多艰苦的工作。如果你经营电子商务，谁会向我支付送货费？哪些人会真正购买这些昂贵的东西？因此，这个国家已经形成了一系列不同的思维方式，这就是为什么它如此充满活力，并且与任何其他全球产品如此不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Fascinating. I could keep going, but I want to talk product. I've collected a bunch of questions from people that know you or people that have worked with you about a bunch of different stuff, so I'm just going to go a little bit all over the place. The first area I wanted to talk about is the user experience. Apparently, you have a interesting insight and a different approach of thinking about new users and new user experiences.
turns.zh: 哇。迷人。我可以继续，但我想谈谈产品。我从认识你的人或与你共事过的人那里收集了很多关于很多不同问题的问题，所以我只想稍微介绍一下。我想谈的第一个领域是用户体验。显然，您对新用户和新用户体验有有趣的见解和不同的思考方法。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: One of the things that I realized once we started working with the products is that product managers and generally, companies are too engrossed in thinking about... because they are very close to the product. It's close to their heart, and they're looking at it all the time. They're looking at a lot of minor nuances in terms of how this works and feels, and almost inherent into this is the bias that everybody is thinking about this product all day, all the time, and so on, and so forth. Whereas the reality is most consumers in the country or in your target market, they don't care, and they may have sometime heard about your product. The word of mouth is not ever so strong, even if you're the strongest brand, and so on, and so forth, but that is the customer that you've got to bring in, and then serve. (00:15:07): So there's very interesting insight that I heard from Scott Belsky from Adobe, and then now, he's doing very interesting stuff, and that stayed with me which was you have to think about users on modern internet consumers having three attributes. So they are lazy, they are vain, and they're selfish. So lazy meaning, "I don't have time for this, so blow my mind away. Otherwise, I'm not going to pay attention." Vain which means, "I have a habit. I'm solving this problem in a particular way, and here, you come with your two-pack product and ask me to change my habit. Do you really expect me to do that?" That's second. That's their inherent attribute. The third one is that they're selfish like, "Show me what's in it for me." (00:15:52): Once you start thinking about users in that vein, and if these users are not even using your product, suddenly, you realize, "Oh my god, it's quite difficult even... How do I attract this kind of customer, and if my marketing team has done a good job at bringing this user to my product, how do I actually now empathize with this lazy, selfish, and vain customer, and build my product in a way so that I can make this appear on your site like this is the thing that you have to use, the way you write your copy, the way you build your onboarding, the way you do your first warm welcome?" It's going to make the biggest amount of change in terms of a product success, then your core product features that you're going to build for your loyal consumers. (00:16:37): So that one insight, and I've seen and applied that multiple times not only the companies that I worked with, the companies I've consulted and spoken with. Most neglect it. Well, they get user onboarding is important, but just how important is that is one, and B, the craft of thinking like a user who's lazy, vain, and selfish, and basically, rejecting all your products, but this does not work for this kind of customer. It's extremely hard. It's very hard, but it's totally worth it if you put that lens on.
turns.zh: 一旦我们开始使用产品，我意识到的一件事是产品经理和一般公司都过于专注于思考......因为他们非常接近产品。它离他们的心很近，他们一直在关注它。他们正在研究其工作原理和感觉方面的许多细微差别，而几乎固有的偏见是每个人都整天、一直在思考这个产品，等等。尽管现实情况是该国或您的目标市场中的大多数消费者并不关心，而且他们有时可能听说过您的产品。口碑并不是那么强大，即使你是最强大的品牌，等等，但这就是你必须引入并服务的客户。 (00:15:07)：我从 Adob​​e 的 Scott Belsky 那里听到了非常有趣的见解，现在他正在做非常有趣的事情，这一点一直困扰着我，那就是你必须考虑具有三个属性的现代互联网消费者中的用户。所以他们是懒惰的，他们是虚荣的，他们是自私的。懒惰的意思是，“我没有时间做这个，所以让我的思想消失。否则，我不会注意。” Vain 的意思是，“我有一个习惯。我正在以一种特定的方式解决这个问题，而在这里，你带着你的两件装产品来要求我改变我的习惯。你真的希望我这样做吗？”那是第二。这是他们与生俱来的属性。第三个是他们很自私，就像“告诉我这对我有什么好处”。 (00:15:52)：一旦你开始以这种方式思考用户，如果这些用户甚至没有使用你的产品，你会突然意识到，“天哪，这甚至相当困难......我如何吸引这种客户，如果我的营销团队在将这个用户吸引到我的产品方面做得很好，那么我现在如何真正同情这个懒惰、自私和虚荣的客户，并以某种方式构建我的产品，以便我可以让它出现在你的网站上，就像这样你必须使用的东西，你编写文案的方式，你建立入职的方式，你第一次热烈欢迎的方式？”它将在产品成功方面做出最大的改变，然后是你将为忠实消费者构建的核心产品功能。 (00:16:37)：这是一种洞察力，我不仅在与我合作过的公司、与我咨询过和交谈过的公司多次看到并应用了这一点。大多数人都忽视了它。嗯，他们让用户入职很重要，但这到底有多重要，一是，二是像懒惰、虚荣和自私的用户一样思考的技巧，基本上，拒绝你的所有产品，但这对这类客户不起作用。这是非常困难的。这很难，但如果你戴上镜头，那就完全值得了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of you using this framework on a product you worked on where you're just like, "Here's a thing we really did..." I don't know, had a big impact or really surprised everyone?
turns.zh: 有没有一个例子，你在你开发的产品上使用这个框架，你会说，“这是我们真正做过的一件事……”我不知道，是否产生了很大的影响，或者真的让每个人都感到惊讶？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: So we used it in two different areas. So one is, of course, products I worked on. So I worked in Swiggy for the last seven years, and really, when we started working towards this user, instead of thinking about everybody as, "This is what our onboarding experience looks like, and this is what our product is." So, essentially, we used, basically, say, a key that it's... "We are a food delivery app. We are a grocery delivery app, and we have these bunch of things." Instead of that, we just started reframing it from the point of view of, "What would you want, and how could you use us? What is it in it for you?" and we started connecting all our marketing messages along with the onboarding. So even going out market and thinking, "Where do you actually find us? How did you know about us? It's a reasonably large brand. Why have you not already downloaded us and used us? Have you used us and rejected us in the past?" So building that entire mental model and looking at a user from the point of view of, "Let's assume that you have heard about us 20 times. What was that exact situation that brought you to download this app?" (00:18:20): So right from the entire journey of you hearing us, what was the trigger, and what was the marketing message, and what was the promotion that we were running? How do we continue that journey on your onboarding from your splash, that 200 rupees of... X rupees if you buy from us, continuing that entire journey in the language that they understand and with the user experience that is continuation from the marketing to product, other thing that we started focusing on a lot more, and it instantly started showing us results. But while I'm talking about just a very simple example and everybody should be doing it, that is true even when you have a particular app which has multiple products and many product lines. It's the same principle that applies there, and that's where I think the largest amount of delta that happens that people don't know really why are we not able to cross-pollinate or cross-sell, and so on, and so forth. (00:19:14): Right now, I'm working with a company called Jupiter which is a financial services app, and it's a neobank. So we care for personal finance, and it has a bunch of offerings. There's a personal account or savings account. There's a credit card. There's mutual funds. There is investments in, say, gold, and FD, and so on, and so forth. It's a bunch of things. But when people think about why using us only for one service and just go away, actually, the key is to recognize that this user has found value in... They are not interested in all the other things that you talked about, so be able to empathize with that user, and now thinking about the behavioral science aspects in terms of, "How do I convert this user from one to the other?" That I think is extremely important.
turns.zh: 所以我们在两个不同的领域使用它。当然，其中之一就是我开发的产品。因此，过去七年我在 Swiggy 工作，实际上，当我们开始针对这个用户工作时，我们并没有将每个人都视为“这就是我们的入门体验，这就是我们的产品”。所以，本质上，我们基本上使用了一个密钥……“我们是一个食品配送应用程序。我们是一个杂货配送应用程序，我们有这些东西。”相反，我们只是开始从以下角度重新构建它：“您想要什么？您如何使用我们？它对您有什么好处？”我们开始将所有营销信息与入职联系起来。因此，即使走出市场并思考，“您实际上在哪里找到我们？您是如何知道我们的？这是一个相当大的品牌。为什么您还没有下载我们并使用我们？您过去是否使用过我们并拒绝过我们？”因此，建立整个心理模型并从以下角度看待用户：“假设您已经听说过我们 20 次。具体是什么情况促使您下载此应用程序？” (00:18:20)：那么从您听到我们讲话的整个过程来看，触发因素是什么，营销信息是什么，我们正在进行的促销活动是什么？我们如何继续你的入职旅程，从你的飞溅，那200卢比……X卢比，如果你从我们这里购买，用他们理解的语言继续整个旅程，并提供从营销到产品的延续的用户体验，这是我们开始关注更多的事情，它立即开始向我们展示结果。但是，虽然我谈论的只是一个非常简单的示例，每个人都应该这样做，但即使您有一个包含多个产品和许多产品线的特定应用程序，情况也是如此。同样的原则也适用于此，我认为这就是最大数量的三角洲发生的地方，人们并不真正知道为什么我们不能异花授粉或交叉销售，等等。 (00:19:14)：现在，我正在与一家名为 Jupiter 的公司合作，这是一家金融服务应用程序，也是一家新银行。所以我们关心个人理财，它有很多产品。有个人帐户或储蓄帐户。有一张信用卡。有共同基金。例如，有黄金、FD 等投资。这是一堆事情。但是，当人们思考为什么只使用我们的一项服务然后就离开时，实际上，关键是要认识到该用户已经发现了价值……他们对您谈到的所有其他事情都不感兴趣，因此能够同情该用户，现在考虑行为科学方面的问题，“我如何将该用户从一个用户转换为另一个用户？”我认为这一点非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a couple things I'm hearing here. One is the importance of focusing on not people currently using your product, but this idea of maybe the marginal user or the adjacent user, the next state of users is who you should be thinking about when you're trying to optimize onboarding the user experience, and then two is... Something that sounds like you've had a lot of success with is picking one value prop, maybe one positioning statement, and then following that through their entire journey versus like, "Here's all the things we do." Is that right?
turns.zh: 我在这里听到了一些事情。一是重要的是不要关注当前使用你产品的人，但这种想法可能是边缘用户或相邻用户，下一个用户状态是你在尝试优化用户体验时应该考虑的人，然后二是......听起来你已经取得了很大成功的事情是选择一个价值支柱，也许是一个定位声明，然后在他们的整个旅程中遵循这一点，而不是像“这就是我们所做的所有事情。”是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: That's absolutely right. Let me give an example of this one. One of the reasons why I really feel product managers must, if not better, but equally understand, category consumers which are not in market or which are not really buying your products just yet. As good as the marketer or the brand expert in your team does... because they really are tasked with, "What is that one message that I can say that will make the user take attention or get to like, 'Oh, this is interesting,' and direct attention towards your product?" If the product managers are able to do that, then they will choose that positioning and essentially, understand, "What is my hope product, and what is the hope that..." At least get them to try my app or any of those things, right? So if they understand it as well as the marketer, and then understand, "Over a period of time, what is the right time when I introduce them to this other one rather than being very greedy about letting the new user try everything?" So that's one. (00:21:37): The other thing that I feel a lot of product managers don't do right is... "Forget about everything. Here's my app. Go figure," is how most of the products are designed unfortunately. Automatically, these things will happen without any intervention. I have created something which is so beautiful, and once you tap that icon, everyone can say, "That is my product that is so working perfectly," but they don't really think about, "At what moment do I actually get this user here, and will they use it?" Well, this user is lazy, vain, and selfish.
turns.zh: 这是绝对正确的。让我举一个例子。我真的觉得产品经理必须（如果不是更好的话）同样理解那些不在市场上或还没有真正购买你的产品的类别消费者的原因之一。就像您团队中的营销人员或品牌专家所做的那样……因为他们的任务实际上是：“我可以说的一条信息是什么，可以让用户引起注意或喜欢，‘哦，这很有趣’，并将注意力转移到您的产品上？”如果产品经理能够做到这一点，那么他们就会选择该定位，并且从本质上理解，“我希望的产品是什么，希望......”至少让他们尝试我的应用程序或任何这些东西，对吧？因此，如果他们和营销人员一样理解它，然后理解，“在一段时间内，什么时候是我向他们介绍另一个产品的合适时机，而不是非常贪婪地让新用户尝试一切？”这就是其中之一。 (00:21:37)：我觉得很多产品经理做得不好的另一件事是......“忘记一切。这是我的应用程序。想想看”，不幸的是，这就是大多数产品的设计方式。这些事情会自动发生，无需任何干预。我创造了一些非常漂亮的东西，一旦你点击那个图标，每个人都可以说，“这就是我的产品，运行得非常完美”，但他们并没有真正考虑，“我什么时候才能真正让这个用户来到这里，他们会使用它吗？”好吧，这个用户是懒惰、虚荣、自私的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That phrase reminds me of something I always think about. Marc Andreessen had this great quote that your user's time is already allocated. They're not looking for more apps to download. They already have a plan for the day. Basically, they have things to do. They're not like, "Hmm, what's another iPhone app I'm going to check out right now?" So somehow you have to convince them, "This is worth your time," and I like this framework. Is there an example of a phrase you found really effective either at Swiggy, or Jupiter, or Flipkart, or anything just like, "Here's a really quick example of something that had a big impact on either simplifying the value prop," or if you don't have an example top of mind, what was the impact you saw from implementing some of these ideas?
turns.zh: 这句话让我想起了我一直在思考的事情。马克·安德森 (Marc Andreessen) 曾说过这样一句话：你的用户的时间已经被分配了。他们并不是在寻找更多的应用程序来下载。他们已经制定了当天的计划。基本上，他们有事情要做。他们不会说，“嗯，我现在要查看的另一个 iPhone 应用程序是什么？”因此，你必须以某种方式说服他们，“这值得你花时间”，而且我喜欢这个框架。是否有一个您发现在 Swiggy、Jupiter、Flipkart 真正有效的短语示例，或者类似的内容，“这是一个对简化价值支柱产生重大影响的非常简单的示例”，或者如果您没有想到示例，那么您在实施其中一些想法时看到了哪些影响？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: I'll talk about a phrase that I now use with product managers a lot to simplify how they should be thinking. I think one thing is... and that's not only for the consumers, but even how we operate. We are product managers, and we are in the business of influence. Users are doing something, and now we want them to do something else. Our engineers are doing something, and now we want to influence them into building something fast. Really, leadership has some plans. We'll influence them to, essentially, look at a plan, and basically, sign off, and do something else. We are in the business of influence, and you are doing this all the time internally. Otherwise, you're not successful even in shipping. Now, we have to extend this to our users and really think about it from that point of view. So you are a full-stack influencer and not only an external influencer. So we've got to think more like sales, more like marketing, more like influencers.
turns.zh: 我将谈论我现在经常与产品经理一起使用的一个短语，以简化他们的思考方式。我认为有一件事是……这不仅关系到消费者，也关系到我们的运营方式。我们是产品经理，我们从事的是影响力行业。用户正在做某事，现在我们希望他们做其他事情。我们的工程师正在做一些事情，现在我们希望影响他们快速构建一些东西。确实，领导层有一些计划。我们将影响他们，从本质上来说，看看一个计划，然后基本上，签字，然后做其他事情。我们从事的是影响力业务，而你们一直在内部这样做。否则，你连发货都不会成功。现在，我们必须将其扩展到我们的用户，并从这个角度真正考虑它。所以你是一个全栈影响者，而不仅仅是一个外部影响者。因此，我们必须更多地从销售、营销、影响者的角度来思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the most important skills for a product manager is influencing people on team, and I like the point that you're also trying to influence your user. That's interesting. Just more reason to get really good at influence, so. I actually have a newsletter about how to get better influence based on Frodo Baggins and Lord of the Rings. We'll link to that in the show notes. Okay. Let's shift to a different topic. You have a really concrete way of actually implementing the working backwards process. We had one of the authors of the book Working Backwards on recently, and I'm excited to just hear what you've learned about how to actually put this into practice. It's easy to hear about, "Let's work backwards," but doing it is a different beast, and so I'd love to hear what you've learned there.
turns.zh: 产品经理最重要的技能之一是影响团队中的人员，我喜欢你也试图影响你的用户这一点。那很有意思。只是更有理由真正擅长影响力，所以。事实上，我有一份关于如何根据弗罗多·巴金斯和《指环王》获得更好影响力的时事通讯。我们将在演出笔记中链接到该内容。好的。让我们换一个话题。您有一种非常具体的方法来实际实施逆向工作过程。最近，我们有一位《向后工作》一书的作者，我很高兴听到您学到了如何将其付诸实践。很容易听到“让我们逆向工作”，但这样做却是另一回事，所以我很想听听您在那里学到了什么。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: So I think the people who invented working backwards is clearly Amazon. I think they started this entire process which are like, "Hey, why don't you write a press release, and with that press release, we'll work backwards from that one?" I thought that was a very cool idea, and I was trying to dig down into like, "Hey, why does it work?" My insight or at least the way that I thought about this one is it's not working backwards only from a customer value proposition. "Will our customers love it, and will they pay for it? Is it noteworthy, and is it something that we should even be working?" While that is one of the most important things that the Working Backwards framework teaches us, but essentially, what you're working backwards from is an entire machinery at a particular day that is working for... For the date of GTM, what do we need to do from here till that particular day so that the GTM is successful, but also, what will be the machinery we would have created so that this product is successful? (00:25:20): Now, because you're already talking about GTM, you're already thinking about, "How will users love it? What is the money that we'll spend? What are the alternatives that we will... routes that we have explored that finally we have zeroed in on and all of those?" So they are all going to be a part of a PR review. If I take a slightly open stance on this one, what is a press release? A press release is you have a one-pager which talks about what are we building, what is a particular date, what is the exact value proposition, what will consumers say, what will the business manager say, how will they respond, how will they use it. But the one thing that comes out from this framework is that you can use it for a whole bunch of other things. You can use it for negotiation, for example, because you start with a date, and then you say, "This is the one-pager that I need to ship, and I want the consumers to see that." You can use it to now go to our VP Engineering and say, "By this date, can we build all of this?" Now, they do not have all the PRDs and everything, but they can give you a sense that this is too aggressive or this is not and so on. (00:26:18): We can also use the quotes here to actually find alliances or find people who are going to actually derail this. So you actually use the customer quote to basically say, "I want my customers to say this. From marketing and from my pricing team, can we actually ship this so that consumers will say that?" Then, from the business owner's quote, you actually say, "This is what we are shipping, but what are your goals? Can you say that within three months, we would have achieved this much?" So using that to build one entire picture is one way that I found it really powerful because if you find disagreements here, then say, "I can't ship it," then you change the date, and then you change the goals because all of these things are changing together. So instead of one, you find the other set of all the things that need to come together for that press release to go live is the real value. (00:27:07): The other part that I found interesting here is that I really truly believe in the power of three. So I actually ask my teams to write three press releases, alternative and divergent like, "What if we..." Suppose you're launching a membership program. So, instead of two tiers, let's do three tiers, or for example, let's take another one which is instead of building a membership, let's build up tiering pricing program with membership points. Instead of this segment, let's use another segment. Let's say within these three, and they all need to be fully thought-through, and that helps the leadership choose. (00:27:44): So the two things that work here. When you are in the product discovery phase, you would have heard from a lot of folks. Finally, if you show them just one roadmap, it feels like, "Hey, this person didn't..." They listened to my interesting point which was valuable, but didn't include it. But when you're doing this three PR FAQs, I considered this, and this added up to a story that eventually is valuable, this alternative route. I considered your point of view, and I created a story, but unfortunately, it is not adding up so we rejected it. So, now, people can compare and contrast, and that's a very powerful leadership tool. That, actually, is a very powerful tool even for CXOs. When they say, "Let's build this," you'll say, "Here are three ways we can build this, and here's the reason why I'm not building what you said because you would like these two more."
turns.zh: 所以我认为发明逆向工作的人显然是亚马逊。我认为他们开始了整个过程，就像是，“嘿，你为什么不写一份新闻稿，然后通过该新闻稿，我们将从那个新闻稿开始倒推？”我认为这是一个非常酷的想法，我试图深入研究，“嘿，为什么它有效？”我的见解，或者至少是我对这个问题的思考方式是，它不仅仅从客户价值主张出发。 “我们的客户会喜欢它吗？他们会为此付费吗？它值得注意吗？这是我们应该努力的事情吗？”虽然这是逆向工作框架教给我们的最重要的事情之一，但本质上，你逆向工作的是在某一特定日期正在工作的整个机器......对于 GTM 的日期，我们需要从现在到那特定的一天做什么才能使 GTM 成功，而且，我们将创建什么机器才能使该产品成功？ (00:25:20)：现在，因为您已经在谈论 GTM，所以您已经在思考，“用户会如何喜欢它？我们会花多少钱？我们会采取哪些替代方案……我们已经探索过的路线，最终我们已经锁定了所有这些路线？”所以它们都将成为公关审查的一部分。如果我对此采取稍微开放的立场，那么什么是新闻稿？新闻稿是一页纸，讨论我们正在构建什么、特定日期是什么、确切的价值主张是什么、消费者会说什么、业务经理会说什么、他们将如何回应、他们将如何使用它。但是这个框架带来的一件事是你可以将它用于很多其他事情。例如，您可以将其用于谈判，因为您从一个日期开始，然后您说：“这是我需要运送的单页寻呼机，我希望消费者看到它。”您现在可以使用它来联系我们的工程副总裁并询问：“到这个日期，我们可以构建所有这些吗？”现在，他们没有所有的 PRD 和一切，但他们可以给你一种感觉，这太激进了，或者这不是，等等。 (00:26:18)：我们还可以使用此处的引言来实际寻找联盟或找到真正会破坏这一情况的人。因此，您实际上使用客户报价基本上是说：“我希望我的客户这么说。从营销和我的定价团队来看，我们实际上可以运送这个产品，以便消费者会这么说吗？”然后，从企业主的引言中，你实际上会说，“这就是我们要发货的东西，但是你的目标是什么？你能说在三个月内，我们会取得这么多成就吗？”因此，用它来构建一幅完整的图画是我发现它非常强大的一种方式，因为如果你在这里发现分歧，然后说，“我不能发货”，然后你改变日期，然后你改变目标，因为所有这些事情都在一起改变。因此，您会发现新闻稿发布所需的另一组所有内容才是真正的价值，而不是其中之一。 (00:27:07)：我发现这里有趣的另一部分是我真的相信三个的力量。所以我实际上要求我的团队写三份新闻稿，不同的和不同的，比如“如果我们......”假设你正在启动一个会员计划。因此，我们不要做两层，而是做三层，或者例如，让我们采取另一层，而不是建立会员资格，让我们用会员积分建立分层定价计划。让我们使用另一个段来代替这个段。比如说这三个，都需要经过深思熟虑，这有助于领导层的选择。 (00:27:44)：所以有两件事在这里起作用。当您处于产品发现阶段时，您会听到很多人的意见。最后，如果你只向他们展示一张路线图，感觉就像是，“嘿，这个人没有……”他们听取了我的有趣观点，这是有价值的，但没有包括在内。但是，当你做这三个公关常见问题解答时，我考虑了这一点，这构成了一个最终有价值的故事，即这条替代路线。我考虑了你的观点，并创作了一个故事，但不幸的是，它不合逻辑，所以我们拒绝了它。所以，现在，人们可以进行比较和对比，这是一个非常强大的领导工具。事实上，即使对于 CXO 来说，这也是一个非常强大的工具。当他们说，“让我们构建这个”时，你会说，“我们可以通过以下三种方式来构建这个，这就是为什么我不构建你所说的方法的原因，因为你还想要这两种。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really cool idea of just using the PR FAQ and working backwards process to think very differently partly to make sure you've explored all the options, partly to just think through things that are in the back of people's minds and see if there's something there before committing to the one direction.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常酷的想法，仅使用公关常见问题解答和逆向工作流程来进行非常不同的思考，部分是为了确保您已经探索了所有选项，部分是为了思考人们脑海中的事情，看看在致力于一个方向之前是否有一些东西。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: So the FAQs also are very important to set processes in the system. For example, now, at Jupiter, we have a financial services app. So every FAQ will mandatorily have, "How are you going to make sure that it is fully compliant? Have you gotten sign-off from A, B, C people? Have you actually thought about legal aspects, and so on, and so forth?" So, for example, you can use the FAQs very effectively here. Whereas, for example, when it was Swiggy, and it's a three-way marketplace, you have consumers, delivery executives, and restaurant partners. Now, any small change that you do on, say, delivery partners, for example, if you're working on optimizing their earnings per hour which will lead to some changes in cost per delivery, but that may have a completely different impact on delivery fee. (00:29:31): I'm just making this up, but now, because of so many moving parts in your FAQs, you're explicitly asking, "Have you thought about what are the implications on restaurant partners? Have you thought about what are implications on delivery partners?" We, in fact, also have that PR FAQ in terms of we write down the different segments of delivery partners, and sometimes it will have extremely weird correlations because those product managers on one side of the equation have started thinking or at least consulting the other part of the marketplace, "What could this mean for you?" It gets everybody together to create very crisp products that work for all sides of the marketplace.
turns.zh: 因此，常见问题解答对于在系统中设置流程也非常重要。例如，现在，在 Jupiter，我们有一个金融服务应用程序。因此，每个常见问题解答都必须包含“您如何确保它完全合规？您是否得到了 A、B、C 人员的签字认可？您是否真正考虑过法律方面的问题等等？”例如，您可以在这里非常有效地使用常见问题解答。然而，例如，当它是 Swiggy 时，它是一个三向市场，有消费者、送货主管和餐厅合作伙伴。现在，您对送货合作伙伴所做的任何小改变，例如，如果您正在努力优化他们的每小时收入，这将导致每次送货成本发生一些变化，但这可能会对送货费用产生完全不同的影响。 (00:29:31)：这只是我编造的，但现在，由于您的常见问题解答中有如此多的变化，您明确地问：“您是否考虑过这对餐厅合作伙伴有何影响？您是否考虑过对送货合作伙伴有何影响？”事实上，我们也有公关常见问题解答，我们写下了交付合作伙伴的不同部分，有时它会产生极其奇怪的相关性，因为等式一侧的那些产品经理已经开始思考或至少咨询市场的另一部分，“这对你意味着什么？”它将每个人聚集在一起，创造出适用于市场各个方面的非常清爽的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One thread I'm pulling out of a few of your stories so far is you often come back to this full-stack approach to many models. So you talked about how PM is like an influencer, but also, they're influencing users. That's a cool way of thinking about it. With this working backwards process, you can use it to think about the full stack of launch, not just what features you're going to build. I know you also have some strong opinions about product managers, and they should be much more full-stack than most PMs. Does that ring a bell, and if so, can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，我从您的一些故事中提取的一条线索是，您经常会回到许多模型的全栈方法。所以你谈到了 PM 如何像一个影响者，而且他们也在影响用户。这是一个很酷的思考方式。通过这个向后工作的过程，您可以用它来考虑启动的完整堆栈，而不仅仅是要构建哪些功能。我知道你对产品经理也有一些强烈的看法，他们应该比大多数产品经理更加全栈。这是否引起了人们的注意？如果是的话，您能谈谈吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yes. No, I think it is the same thread that is connecting the first and the second. I think product managers have to own outcomes and not only features and parts of the problem. Well, they will own some parts of the problem fully, but if they need to work with everybody to make sure that eventual product that they launch is successful and not only successful from the point of view of, "Hey, we launched something that works for users," et cetera, that's not the definition of success. Did it work in the way that it really changed the behavior of the kind of user that we wanted to achieve a business outcome that will build a capability that is important for us? All of those things combined will not happen if the product manager is only thinking about their part. So they have to think about external users, they have to think about competition, they have to think about other product managers and product leaders about engineering, about marketing, and so on because it's such a diverse field. (00:31:36): Unless you really... and I'm not saying you need to be an authority of that. Either you are very, very good at that, or you have built partnerships, and have run your ideas or product through those people and gotten weighted from them, and finally made a decision around that part, I don't think you'll be very successful. So, in my opinion, the full-stack product managers are the ones who are going to be more successful rather than product managers who are doing very good at one particular area only. So there's one book which is Range, right? I'm sure you may have heard about it, right? Even the first chapter, what they talk about is... They take two examples. One is the example of Federer, Roger Federer. So, with Roger Federer, for example, I think I'll just continue that, that till 18, he played a bunch of racket sports, and this wasn't even tennis. But then, you bring in ideas from one racket sport to the other, and second to the third, and so on, and so forth, and now you have such a range of ideas that you can connect a lot more dots and actually ship it. I think that's a better playbook for being more successful in product.
turns.zh: 是的。不，我认为连接第一条和第二条的是同一条线。我认为产品经理必须拥有结果，而不仅仅是问题的特征和部分。好吧，他们将完全承担问题的某些部分，但如果他们需要与每个人合作以确保他们推出的最终产品是成功的，而不仅仅是从“嘿，我们推出了适合用户的东西”等角度来看的成功，那么这不是成功的定义。它的工作方式是否真正改变了我们想要实现的业务成果，从而构建了对我们来说很重要的功能的用户行为？如果产品经理只考虑自己的部分，那么所有这些事情都不会发生。因此，他们必须考虑外部用户，他们必须考虑竞争，他们必须考虑其他产品经理和产品领导者的工程、营销等，因为这是一个如此多样化的领域。 (00:31:36)：除非你真的......而且我并不是说你需要成为这方面的权威。要么你非常非常擅长这一点，要么你已经建立了合作伙伴关系，并通过这些人来运行你的想法或产品并从他们那里获得权重，最后围绕这部分做出了决定，我认为你不会很成功。因此，在我看来，全栈产品经理会比只在某一特定领域表现出色的产品经理更成功。那么有一本书就是《Range》，对吧？我相信你可能听说过，对吧？即使是第一章，他们谈论的也是……他们举了两个例子。一是费德勒的例子，罗杰·费德勒。所以，以罗杰·费德勒为例，我想我会继续这样，直到 18 岁，他参加了一系列球拍运动，而这甚至不是网球。但是，然后，你将想法从一项球拍运动引入另一项运动，然后将第二项运动引入第三项运动，依此类推，现在你有了一系列的想法，你可以连接更多的点并实际交付它。我认为这是在产品方面取得更大成功的更好的策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just watching a documentary on... I think it was called Greatness and had Wayne Gretzky. He had exactly the same experience actually. When he was young, he played hockey just during the winter times, and during summer, he played other sports. Hockey was just like one sport he played, and then eventually started to focus on it, and they talked about how people that played different sports in their childhood actually ended up being much better at that one sport that they chose. So a lot of parallels. I know you also have a lot of interesting ways of thinking about coming up with a roadmap ideas, and ideating and building a roadmap backlog. So you already talked about this idea of going in very divergent directions and seeing if that leads anywhere. There's a couple more someone shared. One is you have this idea of show don't tell. What is that?
turns.zh: 我刚刚在看一部关于……我想它叫《伟大》的纪录片，里面有韦恩·格雷茨基。他实际上也有过完全相同的经历。当他年轻的时候，他只在冬天打曲棍球，夏天则参加其他运动。曲棍球就像他玩的一项运动一样，然后最终开始专注于它，他们谈论了在童年时期参加不同运动的人实际上如何在他们选择的一项运动中表现得更好。所以有很多相似之处。我知道您也有很多有趣的方式来思考提出路线图想法，以及构思和构建路线图积压工作。所以你已经谈到了朝着非常不同的方向前进并看看是否会带来任何结果的想法。还有人分享了一些。一是你有这种“表演而不是讲述”的想法。那是什么？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Actually, show don't tell is an idea which is an extension of what we are talking about from what backwards. When we're talking about working backwards, one is a PR FAQ which is a written documentation of what we are trying to achieve. Show don't tell is essentially a way in where the product manager starts ideating with the entire experience, and they actually create all the collaterals together of a user they need to begin with if you're working on a single-play product which is a single-user product. Then, you actually start bringing together your marketers and others in terms of, "What is literally the first screen, and how is my user getting here?" It's not as simple as he imagines somebody who will be doing this and reaching here. We try to recreate an exact situation. (00:34:16): There's a concept of person, not personas. So we'll talk about personas, but we try to go to, "All right. No. Don't think about agentic user. Let's say Lenny, 30 years old, doing A, B, C things, earning this much, et cetera, et cetera. His relationship with this category of food delivery is X. These are the things that he has done in the last month. In the last three days, there were the needs, desires, aspirations, fears, frustrations, et cetera, et cetera." We say, "Okay. It's 11:00. What's happened? Why is this user open, or what triggered this particular app, and then what happened?" So you literally start from there, and I think 50% of my product reviews are on that part, and then when we say, "All right. Then, this app got open. Do we have the right kind of way forward for Lenny to actually achieve what he came here for?" Literally, each pixel, and each copy, and each word is going to be in service of that part. (00:35:08): So that's showing the entire journey rather than just staying and assuming. So that is something that I've found really powerful with respect to even designing products or even thinking about why are we building something. What it also helps is when we are building complex products, especially in marketplaces because once you are building this for the user, simultaneously, something is happening on the other part if it is simultaneous, if it's a real-time marketplace, or something like that. So you're building something for the user and saying, "All right. If this guy ordered, now there's a 30 minutes time when our delivery executors will come to the user with food. What is happening? What's the emotional state of the user, and let's plot out the 30 minutes time, and let's create various scenarios. Is it like, 'Hey, maybe he went to the restaurant, and the food is delayed,' or the dude on a bike, his bike got punctured, et cetera. Now, what is the consumer thinking at this time?" So you show all of those things in real time, and that cuts out a whole bunch of random ways in which the product could have looked like if you're creating even a chatbot. So just having that showcase of all journeys coming together helps a lot in building your products in the right way.
turns.zh: 实际上，“表演而不是讲述”是一个想法，它是我们所讨论的内容向后延伸的一个想法。当我们谈论逆向工作时，其中一个是公关常见问题解答，它是我们试图实现的目标的书面文档。展示而不讲述本质上是产品经理开始构思整个体验的一种方式，如果您正在开发单人产品（即单用户产品），他们实际上会一起创建他们需要开始的所有用户资料。然后，您实际上开始将营销人员和其他人聚集在一起，讨论“第一个屏幕实际上是什么？我的用户如何到达这里？”这并不像他想象的那么简单，有人会这样做并到达这里。我们尝试重现一个确切的情况。 (00:34:16)：有一个人的概念，而不是角色。所以我们会讨论人物角色，但我们会尝试去说，“好吧。不。不要考虑代理用户。假设 Lenny，30 岁，做 A、B、C 的事情，赚了这么多，等等。他与此类送餐的关系是 X。这些是他在上个月所做的事情。在过去的三天里，有需求、欲望、愿望、恐惧、挫败感等。诸如此类，等等。”我们说，“好吧。现在是 11:00。发生了什么？为什么这个用户打开，或者是什么触发了这个特定的应用程序，然后发生了什么？”所以你真的从那里开始，我认为我 50% 的产品评论都在这一部分，然后当我们说，“好吧。然后，这个应用程序开放了。我们是否有正确的前进方向，让莱尼真正实现他来这里的目的？”从字面上看，每个像素、每个副本、每个单词都将为该部分服务。 (00:35:08)：所以这展示了整个旅程，而不仅仅是停留和假设。因此，我发现这对于设计产品或什至思考我们为什么要构建某些东西来说非常强大。它还有帮助的是，当我们构建复杂的产品时，尤其是在市场中，因为一旦你为用户构建这个产品，同时，另一部分就会发生一些事情，如果它是同时发生的，如果它是实时市场，或者类似的东西。所以你正在为用户构建一些东西，并说：“好吧。如果这个人点了餐，现在我们的送货执行者将在 30 分钟内给用户送食物。发生了什么？用户的情绪状态如何，让我们规划出这 30 分钟的时间，然后创建各种场景。是不是像，‘嘿，也许他去了餐厅，食物被延误了’，或者骑自行车的家伙，他的自行车得到了刺穿等等。现在，消费者此时在想什么？”因此，您可以实时显示所有这些内容，并且如果您正在创建聊天机器人，那么就消除了产品可能看起来的一大堆随机方式。因此，仅仅展示所有旅程的结合对于以正确的方式构建您的产品有很大帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, essentially, just getting very detailed and very concrete with the product experience that you're building thinking about the user experience. Sounds like a lot of work. I can't imagine you do this often. Is the advice here to do this once a year or once and just keep it updated? It sounds like you did this at Swiggy, and that was a really impactful way of building the product.
turns.zh: 因此，从本质上讲，只需非常详细和具体地了解您正在构建的产品体验，并考虑用户体验。听起来工作量很大。我无法想象你经常这样做。这里的建议是每年执行一次还是一次并保持更新？听起来您在 Swiggy 就是这样做的，这是构建产品的一种非常有影响力的方式。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yeah. I think there's not only one way actually. I think I recommend this every product manager to do a show don't tell version of their current version. At the same time, there's a new version all the time. So they can compare and contrast, and very easily explain to everyone why they're doing something. In fact, that wall... So it's called a wall. It also becomes one common place where you can get all the stakeholders in because it becomes... Instead of just doing the elevator pitch, you can actually do detailed discussions on why I'm choosing this versus something else, and so on, and so forth. That's a product manager's version of doing this. (00:37:10): There's also a product leader's version of doing this thing which is recycle strategy on a page, and a lot of people call it like growth loops. Right? Don't show our user's journey. Now, let's see the entire strategy of the company together on one page. "All right. This is what the market looks like, and why will we get what kind of users? What is our activation budgets, and how many of them are we going to get to this next stage and get them to use it? How will we get them to cross-pollinate into different sections? Do we need a membership program? Are there any different levers which will press more or less and so on?" So that also is a show don't tell, and not only one, but usually, I like to create three of them as well like, "Why did we choose a strategy versus the other?" That, for example, is a very good way for our product leaders to get to one strategy that their CXOs align with and something that they can essentially tell the entire product and other teams, "This is what we're going to follow."
turns.zh: 是的。我认为实际上不止一种方法。我想我建议每个产品经理都做一个展示，不要告诉他们当前版本的版本。与此同时，不断有新版本出现。这样他们就可以进行比较和对比，并且很容易地向每个人解释他们为什么要做某事。其实那堵墙……所以才叫墙。它也成为一个常见的地方，你可以让所有利益相关者参与其中，因为它变得……你不仅可以进行电梯游说，还可以详细讨论为什么我选择这个而不是其他东西，等等。这是产品经理的做法。 (00:37:10)：还有一个产品负责人的版本，即页面上的回收策略，很多人称之为增长循环。正确的？不要展示我们用户的旅程。现在，让我们在一页上一起看到公司的整个战略。 “好吧。这就是市场的样子，为什么我们会吸引什么样的用户？我们的激活预算是多少，我们要进入下一阶段并让他们使用多少用户？我们如何让他们交叉授粉到不同的部分？我们是否需要会员计划？是否有任何不同的杠杆可以或多或少地施加压力等等？”因此，这也是一个无法讲述的节目，不仅是一个，而且通常，我也喜欢创建其中三个，例如“为什么我们选择一种策略而不是另一种策略？”例如，对于我们的产品负责人来说，这是一种非常好的方法，可以让他们的 CXO 制定出符合的策略，并且他们基本上可以告诉整个产品和其他团队，“这就是我们要遵循的策略。”
