turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: I think the largest impact that happens here is on alignment, so how CXOs are thinking if that is not very clear, and that can be a document, and so on, and so forth. But for a lot of people, it's not very clear on... I can see one part of the funnel. I can understand... The marketing team can understand the best why we are acquiring those users, but they don't fully see the picture of, "If I attract this kind of users, why will these users become loyal, and what does that entire thing look like or, say, some other team which is building a part of the product? Where do I come in and so on?" So I think the largest impact that the show don't tell has is on, basically, getting the entire company together on the same page and them being able to understand why I'm doing, and which part of the entire picture I am working on, and why others are working on so that I can actually work with them to solve that part. That's one. (00:40:30): The other thing that it helps, Lenny, is it also helps in choosing directions, like I said, because we are not doing one, but three of them. I'm choosing one alternative versus the other, and sometimes these strategic discussions, they can get going all sorts of different ways, and maybe you will talk about one particular unique point and go deeper rather than look at the entire picture together and say, "This is good because of all of these five points that we presented in page one versus the other one."
turns.zh: 我认为这里发生的最大影响是一致性，如果这不是很清楚的话，CXO 是如何思考的，这可以是一个文档，等等。但对于很多人来说，这并不是很清楚……我可以看到漏斗的一部分。我可以理解……营销团队最能理解我们为什么要获取这些用户，但他们并没有完全了解“如果我吸引了这类用户，为什么这些用户会变得忠诚，整个事情是什么样子，或者说，其他一些团队正在构建产品的一部分？我从哪里进来等等？”所以我认为这部剧没有讲述的最大影响基本上是让整个公司聚集在同一页面上，他们能够理解我为什么这样做，我正在研究整个图片的哪一部分，以及为什么其他人正在研究，这样我就可以真正与他们合作解决该部分。这是一个。 (00:40:30)：莱尼，它的另一件事是它也有助于选择方向，就像我说的，因为我们不是在做一个，而是三个。我选择一种替代方案而不是另一种方案，有时这些战略讨论可以以各种不同的方式进行，也许你会谈论一个特定的独特点并进行更深入的讨论，而不是一起看整个图片并说：“这很好，因为我们在第一页和另一页中提出了所有这五点。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the other benefit, just one of the benefits of working backwards in Amazon's whole written-down memo approach is it forces you to crystallize ideas and not stay superficial because there's so many good ideas in theory. But then, when you have to get really concrete, that's actually a terrible idea. Basically, it's the same benefit in a lot of ways of get very concrete. What are you actually going to do? That will help you identify, "Okay. This isn't going to work. What are we even thinking?" So I like that. Awesome. Okay. Another framework that you have is something that you call the four BB framework for product strategy. Can you talk about what that's all about?
turns.zh: 我认为另一个好处，只是亚马逊整个书面备忘录方法中逆向工作的好处之一，它迫使你具体化想法，而不是停留在肤浅的层面上，因为理论上有很多好想法。但是，当你必须变得非常具体时，这实际上是一个糟糕的主意。基本上，它在很多方面都有同样的好处，而且非常具体。你实际上打算做什么？这将帮助你识别，“好吧。这行不通。我们到底在想什么？”所以我喜欢这样。惊人的。好的。您拥有的另一个框架被称为产品战略的四个 BB 框架。你能谈谈这到底是怎么回事吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: We essentially saw that if a startup actually usually wants to do a bunch of things across the border, there's always like, "Hey, I should be investing in tech debt or building core platforms. That would really help my product in the long term. That's super important," and that's my engineering managers and largely, people asking for that bandwidth. Then, there is the product manager themselves who's basically saying, "I want to do feature enhancement, bug fixes, my version twos, a few areas, experiments, and so on, and so forth." That's a regular product backlog that would work on screen by screen, and there's this leadership which will say, "You know what? Now, we have a suite of products. Now, I want to take a large delta bit that may work. It may not work, but we need to make sure that it works, but I need work across teams, and it's not only one person that needs to do it. I need contribution from four or five of you that come together and deliver that," or there are places where a company is just reimagining their identity, or they're pivoting which is like, "All right. We were doing X. Now, we are doing X plus Y. That's how we want to be known," or, "We were doing X. Now, we want to do very little of X because current consumers, okay, we will take care of them, but now we want to pivot into Y." (00:42:55): So it usually is in four of these buckets, and what really happens is it gets down to product managers eventually prioritizing between these four. So I don't think it's a tactical prioritization product manager call. It really is a product strategy call, and the conversation that needs to happen is between, say, the head of product and the CEO or even the leadership. If I gave you a hundred focus points, how much will you put in each of these buckets, and what are those four buckets? Those are the four BB buckets, so what are the ones? We call them... First BB is Brilliant Basics. The reason why we call it BB, Brilliant Basic, you need to brand... You cannot brand it as tech debt, so it feels like very off because these are brilliant, these are important. That's what the company's built on, and the company needs to invest in that. So that's one. (00:43:46): The second one is Bread and Butter. So that's your backlogs. If the product managers had no big ideas, and they just were left on their own, what would they come up with in terms of just improving that line of business that they're given? Then, there are Big Bets. Now, that's where your larger ideas that have come together, but how many big bets should we take, or is this big bet even a big one? That's where you're working backwards or PR FAQs start becoming even more important because those are the kind of bets that cannot be taken without everybody basically signing up, working backwards, and saying, "We will all make this successful." (00:44:26): Breaking Bad essentially is a different world altogether. That's where you want to redefine your company. For example, in Swiggy, if we were doing food delivery, now we want to do grocery delivery as well. It's like these are two companies working together, or from a food delivery company, we wanted to become a convenience company. So that's almost breaking bad. Again, like I said, we got cheesy, but the good thing that happens is now what you can do is, along with your leadership, take stock, and the head of product essentially can say, "You know what? In the next year, I can invest a lot less on my brilliant basics, and we should as a company focus a lot on this breaking back because that is existential." But then, we should not look back and say, "Why were tech systems a little bit broken this time? We had a little bit more down times." (00:45:17): You can basically blow it out and almost showcase what to expect. For example, if we are just working on a whole bunch of bread and butters, so you'll start seeing a lot fewer bugs, customers will be a little happier. You worked a lot more... drill in basics. Tech systems are nice, but you didn't create any differentiators. Well, none of your bets went out, and your competitors are catching up. So does that sound like a better future? These are hard questions, and these privatization questions... I don't think of product management questions so much as product strategy questions, but in a lot of cases, executors don't know what they're trading off against. (00:45:53): So if you are able to create the conversation around which buckets do we want to put in and create three alternatives... I have tried to do that a bunch of times. Let's look at strategy A, and we see how to be divergent. Suppose we were putting a lot fewer focus points in brilliant basics and a lot more on, for example, big bets, then there will be a risk that they will be like, "We won't have any experiments or very less experiments. Bugs will stay bugs, but we will get a shot at changing the game." Is that a future that sounds better or something else which is like because you're pained also by a lot of bugs and constant down times, which is more secure, but we won't build something amazing, so which sounds better? Because you are able to drive that, now the clarity to the product managers is way clearer in terms of what will they do. Also, they would know that if they have been signed up for a big bet, then they will need to contribute to the PR FAQ. They will need to contribute to the actual working on that irrespective of what their product was, but now they're part of something bigger.
turns.zh: 我们基本上看到，如果一家初创公司实际上通常想要跨境做很多事情，那么总是会这样，“嘿，我应该投资技术债务或构建核心平台。从长远来看，这确实对我的产品有帮助。这是非常重要的，”这就是我的工程经理和很大程度上要求这种带宽的人。然后，产品经理自己基本上会说：“我想做功能增强、错误修复、我的版本二、一些领域、实验等等。”这是一个常规的产品积压工作，会在屏幕上逐个屏幕地工作，领导层会说，“你知道吗？现在，我们有一套产品。现在，我想要采取可能有效的大增量。它可能行不通，但我们需要确保它有效，但我需要跨团队工作，而且需要的不仅仅是一个人。我需要四五个人的贡献，齐心协力并交付它，”或者在某些地方，公司只是重新构想他们的身份，或者他们正在转向，“好吧。我们正在做 X。现在，我们正在做 X 加 Y。这就是我们想要被认识的方式，”或者，“我们正在做 X。现在，我们想做很少的 X，因为当前的消费者，好吧，我们会照顾他们，但现在我们想转向 Y。” (00:42:55)：所以它通常分为四个类别，而真正发生的情况是产品经理最终在这四个类别之间确定优先级。所以我不认为这是产品经理的战术优先级呼吁。这实际上是一次产品战略电话会议，需要在产品主管和首席执行官甚至领导层之间进行对话。如果我给你一百个焦点，你会在每个桶中投入多少，这四个桶是什么？这是四个 BB 桶，那么是哪些呢？我们称它们为……First BB 是 Brilliant Basics。我们之所以称之为 BB，Brilliant Basic，你需要品牌化……你不能将其品牌化为技术债务，所以感觉很不对劲，因为这些很出色，这些很重要。这就是公司的基础，公司需要对此进行投资。这就是其中之一。 (00:43:46)：第二个是《面包和黄油》。这就是您的积压订单。如果产品经理没有什么伟大的想法，他们只能靠自己，那么他们会想出什么来改进他们所分配的业务线呢？然后，还有大赌注。现在，这就是你更大的想法聚集在一起的地方，但我们应该下多少大赌注，或者这个大赌注甚至是一个大赌注？这就是你要逆向工作的地方，或者公关常见问题解答开始变得更加重要，因为如果没有每个人基本上都签名、逆向工作并说“我们都会让这件事成功”，那么这些赌注是不可能进行的。 (00:44:26)：《绝命毒师》本质上是一个完全不同的世界。这就是您想要重新定义您的公司的地方。例如，在 Swiggy，如果我们从事食品配送，现在我们也想做杂货配送。就好像这是两家公司一起合作，或者从一家食品配送公司，我们想成为一家便利公司。所以这几乎是坏事。再说一次，就像我说的，我们变得俗气，但现在发生的好事是，你现在可以做的是，在你的领导力的帮助下，进行盘点，产品负责人基本上可以说，“你知道吗？明年，我可以减少对我出色的基础产品的投资，作为一家公司，我们应该重点关注这种突破，因为这是事关生存的。”但是，我们不应该回头说：“为什么这次技术系统有点坏了？我们的停机时间多了一点。” (00:45:17)：你基本上可以把它吹出来并几乎展示出预期的结果。例如，如果我们只是在生产一大堆面包和黄油，那么您会开始看到更少的错误，客户会更高兴一些。你做了更多的工作...基础知识的练习。技术系统很好，但你没有创造任何差异化因素。好吧，你的赌注都没有兑现，而你的竞争对手正在迎头赶上。那么这听起来像是一个更美好的未来吗？这些都是难题，这些私有化问题……我认为产品管理问题不如产品策略问题，但在很多情况下，执行者不知道他们要权衡什么。 (00:45:53)：所以，如果你能够围绕我们想要放入哪些存储桶创建对话并创建三个替代方案......我已经尝试过很多次了。让我们看看策略A，看看如何发散。假设我们在出色的基础知识上投入了更少的关注点，而更多地投入到大赌注等方面，那么他们就会有这样的风险：“我们不会进行任何实验或很少进行实验。错误将永远是错误，但我们将尝试改变游戏规则。”这是一个听起来更好的未来，还是其他一些听起来更好的东西，因为你也因为很多错误和持续的停机时间而痛苦，这更安全，但我们不会构建一些令人惊奇的东西，所以哪个听起来更好？因为你能够推动这一点，所以现在产品经理更清楚他们要做什么。此外，他们会知道，如果他们已经注册了一个大赌注，那么他们将需要为公关常见问题解答做出贡献。无论他们的产品是什么，他们都需要为实际工作做出贡献，但现在他们是更大事业的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I love it. Okay. So just to summarize so people can have just a very short definition of this framework. Brilliant Basics is essentially tech debt and things that you just have to do like hygiene almost. Bread and Butter is essentially optimizing the product, existing product. Big Bets are big bets, and Breaking Bad are just future big rocket like moon shots just transform the way the business works?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我喜欢它。好的。总结一下，这样人们就可以对这个框架有一个非常简短的定义。辉煌的基础本质上是技术债务和你只需要做的事情，比如卫生。 Bread and Butter 本质上是在优化产品、现有产品。大赌注就是大赌注，《绝命毒师》只是未来的大火箭，就像登月一样，只是改变了商业运作的方式？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. It's also interesting. Another thread that comes up again and again in your advice is exploring all the options before committing to one like you always... I think it sounds like you always try to recommend three. I guess let me say what I always find is important there is I think it's important for the product manager to recommend one along with that. It's not just like, "Here's three. You tell me which one you do." It's like, "Here's three. Here's my recommendation why." Is that your advice too, or do you see something-
turns.zh: 我喜欢它。这也很有趣。您的建议中一次又一次出现的另一个主题是在像往常一样做出选择之前探索所有选项……我认为听起来您总是尝试推荐三个。我想让我说一下我一直认为很重要的一点，我认为产品经理推荐一个也很重要。这不仅仅是“这是三个。你告诉我你做哪一个。”就像，“这是三个。这是我的推荐原因。”这也是你的建议吗，还是你看到了什么——

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: 100%, 100%. So when you have explored the three, you essentially have done the work one like, "I have covered all bases and also crystallized them into a concrete option. Now, I'm choosing one on the company's behalf on the basis of whatever I know about the market, about the company, about our strategy, and about how we will make it successful." Now, if I miss something, it's also a time where you can actually work with leadership and other product managers to essentially get that knowledge complete, or if you're 80% right, you can actually use elements of strategy two and strategy three to bring into one. So that's always the way that your thing that... one very concrete option, but because you have these other tools so that you're not missing and bringing it together. But ultimately, you're the one who is going to champion this, and that's where the other leadership element of Amazon comes in which is disagree and commit. But once we have aligned on this one, we'll all commit to launching this, and then the leadership should not go back and forth on that part.
turns.zh: 100%，100%。因此，当你探索了这三者之后，你基本上就完成了一项工作，比如“我已经涵盖了所有基础，并将它们具体化为一个具体的选择。现在，我根据我对市场、公司、我们的战略以及我们如何使其成功的了解，代表公司选择一个。”现在，如果我错过了什么，你也可以与领导层和其他产品经理实际合作，从根本上完成这些知识，或者如果你的正确率达到 80%，你实际上可以使用策略二和策略三的要素将其整合到一起。所以这始终是你的事情......一个非常具体的选择，但因为你有这些其他工具，所以你不会错过并将它们组合在一起。但最终，你是那个要拥护这一点的人，这就是亚马逊的另一个领导元素的用武之地，即不同意和承诺。但一旦我们在这一问题上达成一致，我们都会致力于启动这一项目，然后领导层就不应该在这方面来回摇摆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to go in a completely different direction. It feels like you have a lot of contrarian opinions about how to build product, and how to build teams, and build companies, and things like that, so I just want to start broad. What are some things you have contrarian opinions about, things you believe that a lot of other people maybe don't believe or seek differently?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我想走向一个完全不同的方向。感觉你对如何构建产品、如何构建团队、如何创建公司等等有很多相反的观点，所以我只想从广泛的角度开始。您对哪些事情有相反的看法，您认为很多其他人可能不相信或有不同的寻求？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: So one, for example, excellence and speed. There's always a question around that. "Hey, would you rather ship faster, or would you rather ship better?" In my opinion, when you have to make a choice, think more and ship better. Most experiments should be thought experiments. They should not even be tried out because they're obviously going to fail which is contrary to, "Let's try it out, and then let's see." I think that wastes a lot of company time. If you had smart people who could do metathinking, a lot of experiments would just not even be like... It's not a rule, but it's a preference. I think speed and excellence are two different axes. Ideally, you should be better at both, but if you had to choose one, choose excellence. (00:50:04): There's another contrarian opinion which is... I think most product managers, and again, I'm probably talking a little bit of the kind of people that I work with and have interacted with in product. Most product managers should not even be product managers. They should think a little bit more around whether this is actually the right field for them because I think a lot of people from other areas have entered the field without fully realizing what it takes. So there is definitely a way in which you can coach yourself, and then work your way upwards of that one, but it can make you quite miserable if it's not right for you.
turns.zh: 例如，卓越和速度。总是有一个问题围绕着这个问题。 “嘿，你愿意运送得更快，还是运送得更好？”在我看来，当你必须做出选择时，多思考并提供更好的服务。大多数实验应该是思想实验。它们甚至不应该被尝试，因为它们显然会失败，这与“让我们尝试一下，然后看看”相反。我认为这浪费了很多公司时间。如果你有聪明的人可以进行元思考，那么很多实验就不会像……这不是规则，而是一种偏好。我认为速度和卓越是两个不同的轴。理想情况下，你应该在这两方面都做得更好，但如果你必须选择其中之一，那就选择卓越。 (00:50:04)：还有另一种相反的观点，那就是……我认为大多数产品经理，再说一次，我可能会谈论一些与我一起工作并在产品中与之互动的人。大多数产品经理甚至不应该成为产品经理。他们应该更多地思考这是否真的适合他们，因为我认为很多来自其他领域的人已经进入这个领域，但没有完全意识到它需要什么。所以肯定有一种方法可以让你自我指导，然后继续努力向上，但如果它不适合你，它会让你非常痛苦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something folks should look for there that will tell them you probably shouldn't be a product manager? Either motivation, or skill set, or background, or anything?
turns.zh: 人们应该在那里寻找一些东西来告诉他们你可能不应该成为产品经理？要么是动机，要么是技能，要么是背景，还是其他什么？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: No. I don't think about particular domains that you come from. I have, again, a simple framework of three. I think the first thing is essentially raw sharps, and that can manifest itself into problem identification and problem solving. That's one, and also, higher-order thinking and all of that. I think that is super important. The second one is what I call drive or grit. I think with that comes a whole bunch of qualities around curiosity, learnability, never giving up, consumer-backward thinking, "I really want to solve this," and all of that that comes with that. Third, which is a little difference, we talked about that, is influence. You're in the business of influence, and if you can see yourself that, "I'm built this way," or, "I want to really get better at these," that's when I think this field is going to serve you well.
turns.zh: 不，我不会考虑您来自的特定领域。我再次有一个简单的三个框架。我认为第一件事本质上是原始锐利，这可以体现在问题识别和解决问题上。这就是其中之一，也是高阶思维等等。我认为这非常重要。第二个是我所说的动力或毅力。我认为随之而来的是好奇心、学习能力、永不放弃、消费者落后思维、“我真的想解决这个问题”等一系列品质，所有这些都随之而来。第三，我们谈到了一点区别，那就是影响力。你从事的是影响力行业，如果你能看到自己，“我就是这样构建的”，或者“我真的想在这些方面做得更好”，那么我认为这个领域将会很好地为你服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that everything is three. How handy.
turns.zh: 我喜欢一切都是三的。多么方便啊。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Only the BBs are four. I wish I could compress them three.
turns.zh: 只有 BB 是四个。我希望我能把它们压缩成三个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. There's too many things to do there. Essentially, these are maybe your perspective on the most important PM skills. A good way to think about it. Influence, grit, and just being smart.
turns.zh: 是的。那里有太多事情要做。从本质上讲，这些可能是您对最重要的 PM 技能的看法。一个很好的思考方式。影响力、勇气和聪明。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what you said here is not like you have to be amazing at these to get into product and do well. It's you need to be excited about getting better at these skills.
turns.zh: 我认为你在这里所说的并不是说你必须在这些方面表现出色才能进入产品并做得很好。你需要对提高这些技能感到兴奋。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yes. That's right.
turns.zh: 是的。这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 惊人的。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Well, I think it's not as if that everybody is born with a lot of influence. Of course, you can get better at it, but it's a prospect of that, "Hey, I will need to be influential to succeed at this job." That should excite you and not scare you away. You should not think like, "Hey, you know what? I can get away from this and still be very successful product manager," because most likely, you will not.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为并不是每个人生来就有很大的影响力。当然，你可以做得更好，但这是一个前景，“嘿，我需要有影响力才能在这份工作上取得成功。”这应该会让你兴奋而不是吓跑你。你不应该这样想：“嘿，你知道吗？我可以摆脱这个，并且仍然是非常成功的产品经理，”因为很可能你不会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe spending a little more time here. So, smart, you're probably not going to be able to do a lot about. In terms of grit or influence, is there anything you can share about what you've seen most helps people develop at these skills other than just doing the job for a while, and then starting to get better at this?
turns.zh: 也许在这里多花一点时间。所以，聪明的，你可能无能为力。就勇气或影响力而言，您是否可以分享一下您所看到的最能帮助人们发展这些技能的东西，而不仅仅是做一段时间的工作，然后开始做得更好？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yeah. I think even smartness, I think 80% of that smartness, I think, is something that's very achievable. You don't need to be outstanding on that. Domain knowledge, for example, is something just like... An average smart person with no domain knowledge versus you armed with a lot of knowledge around domain and so on can already take you there, but you can take better decisions. I think first one is more about decision-making, problem identification, problem solving, and all of that. So I think that really can be developed at least to a level where you are very effective. Drive, I think, is probably the hardest to coach, probably the hardest. I've not seen people with less drive actually eventually turning out with a lot of drive, et cetera, but they can be inspired. I think you need to be a person who can think about it that way, but the third one, influences, I think, there's no negotiation there. You need to really think that, "I have to be good at this one." (00:53:46): There's another framework that, Lenny, I wanted to talk about. When I look at product leadership in general and how do you think about different people and so on. When is it a product manager problem, or your problem, or a company problem? There are only three reasons, again, why things do not happen the way you want them to happen as a leader. You can look at a person, and you would say either that person can't do, which is a capability issue, or they won't do, which is a motivation or an alignment issue, or they were not set up to do, which is really your problem, that you didn't set up the ways of working now design properly, or we are okay as such and such, and so on, and so forth. (00:54:26): So, as a leader, it's almost the opposite of what we talked about, great influence and raw sharps. Do you have the right people in terms of capability? If not, is the right answer for us to coach them or to really put them... or mentor them and so on, or move them to some other place because maybe their capability is suited elsewhere? If they won't do, why won't they? Are they not aligned to you? Do they not agree with your vision? Do they not just have enough time? So on and so forth. So you need to really go deeper there. Why won't they do? (00:55:05): There are different answers for that, but if it's a setup issue, and at least I've realized that apart from what product managers can do, almost 70%, 80% of problems why things don't happen are a setup issue. Product leaders or other leaders have not thought through what OKRs are doing to my company, not really fully thought through around org design. If you've read the book called TEEN Topologies, that's one interesting book which starts with Conway's law and essentially saying, "Show me an engineering architecture, and I will actually tell you what the org design of this company is," but that also manifests itself in products that you can basically look at a product. In most cases, you will be able to say what was org design that led to this kind of product.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为即使是聪明，我认为 80% 的聪明也是可以实现的。你不需要在这方面表现出色。例如，领域知识就像……一个没有领域知识的普通聪明人与拥有大量领域知识的你相比，已经可以带你到达那里，但你可以做出更好的决策。我认为第一个更多的是关于决策、问题识别、问题解决等等。所以我认为至少可以发展到非常有效的水平。我认为，驾驶可能是最难教练的，也可能是最难的。我还没有看到那些动力不足的人最终会变得动力十足，等等，但他们可以受到启发。我认为你需要成为一个能够这样思考的人，但第三个，影响，我认为，那里没有谈判。你需要认真思考，“我必须擅长这一点。” (00:53:46)：Lenny，我想谈谈另一个框架。当我总体上看待产品领导力以及你如何看待不同的人等等时。什么时候是产品经理的问题，还是你的问题，还是公司的问题？同样，事情没有按照你作为领导者希望的方式发生的原因只有三个。你可以看着一个人，你会说，要么那个人不能做，这是一个能力问题，要么他们不会做，这是一个动机或一致性问题，或者他们没有被设置去做，这实际上是你的问题，你没有正确设置现在设计的工作方式，或者我们这样等等都可以，等等。 (00:54:26)：所以，作为领导者，这几乎与我们谈论的相反，巨大的影响力和原始的锐利。就能力而言，您是否拥有合适的人员？如果不是，那么正确的答案是我们指导他们或真正安置他们......或指导他们等等，或者将他们转移到其他地方，因为也许他们的能力适合其他地方？如果他们不做，为什么不做？他们与你不一致吗？他们不同意你的愿景吗？他们的时间还不够吗？等等。所以你需要真正深入那里。他们为什么不这样做？ (00:55:05)：对此有不同的答案，但如果这是一个设置问题，至少我已经意识到，除了产品经理可以做的事情之外，几乎 70%、80% 的事情没有发生的问题都是设置问题。产品领导者或其他领导者没有思考 OKR 对我的公司做了什么，没有真正充分思考组织设计。如果你读过《TEEN Topologies》这本书，那是一本有趣的书，它从康威定律开始，本质上是说，“给我展示一个工程架构，我实际上会告诉你这家公司的组织设计是什么”，但这也体现在产品中，你基本上可以看到一个产品。在大多数情况下，您将能够说出是什么组织设计导致了此类产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have heard that book mentioned a couple of times recently. I got to check it out just to the three you just shared, which is another three. I love it. Can do, won't do. What was the third one again, didn't do?
turns.zh: 我最近多次听到有人提到这本书。我只检查了你刚才分享的三个，这是另外三个。我喜欢它。能做，不会做。第三个又是什么，没做？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Not set up to do.
turns.zh: 没有设置做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not set up to do. That one is long. That's a long one. I think what's cool about these are they're essentially ways to measure performance. Maybe if you're a product manager, like performance reviews, it's like, "Did you have the skills to do this? Did you have the motivation to do this, or is it something not set up for you?" You weren't set up for success, basically?
turns.zh: 没有设置做。那个很长。那是一篇很长的文章。我认为这些的最酷之处在于它们本质上是衡量性能的方法。也许如果你是一名产品经理，就像绩效评估一样，“你有能力做到这一点吗？你有动机这样做吗？或者这不是为你设置的吗？”基本上，你还没有为成功做好准备？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's go to AI corner, something I'm trying to do with every guest. Is there anything you've learned about working with AI that you think might be helpful to listeners?
turns.zh: 好的。让我们去人工智能角吧，这是我试图与每位客人一起做的事情。您认为在使用人工智能方面学到的任何东西可能对听众有帮助吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yeah. I think a couple of things. I think working with AI, many, many teams and companies get too excited about AI, and the possibilities, and so on, and it's almost like a solution ready to find a problem within their companies, which also is fine because now you're thinking about possibilities on what this particular technology can do for my company. So it's a good way to start, but many people don't actually use it in the best way possible and force fit it. Instead of that, you can think about, "How do I get AI to work with HI?" Again, it's connecting back with... and this is something that Swiggy CEO, Sriharsha, invented this term called HI just to make sure that everybody understands. (00:57:13): Artificial intelligence is important as much as human intelligence. If you're not humanly intelligent, you're not going to be artificially intelligent or AI really help your company a lot. So, literally, any product that you're building, even when it is technologically quite interesting, and exciting, and so on, it needs to be balanced out and work together along with a great UX, along with behavioral science. The combination of those two will actually make sure that you're getting the best outcome of that, unless you are building something which is completely backed and with no human interventions. We're talking about consumer products largely.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为有几件事。我认为在与人工智能合作时，许多团队和公司对人工智能及其可能性等感到过于兴奋，这几乎就像一个准备好在公司内部发现问题的解决方案，这也很好，因为现在你正在考虑这种特定技术可以为我的公司做些什么的可能性。所以这是一个很好的开始方式，但很多人实际上并没有以尽可能最好的方式使用它并强行适应它。相反，你可以思考“如何让 AI 与 HI 一起工作？”再说一次，它与……联系在一起，这是 Swiggy 首席执行官 Sriharsha 发明的这个术语，称为 HI，只是为了确保每个人都能理解。 (00:57:13)：人工智能与人类智能一样重要。如果你没有人类智慧，你就不会成为人工智能，或者人工智能不会真正为你的公司带来很多帮助。因此，从字面上看，您正在构建的任何产品，即使它在技术上非常有趣、令人兴奋等，也需要平衡并与出色的用户体验和行为科学一起工作。这两者的结合实际上将确保您获得最佳结果，除非您正在构建完全支持并且没有人为干预的东西。我们主要讨论的是消费品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've helped build some of the most successful marketplaces in India and in the world. I'm curious just what may be a lesson or two about building a successful marketplace?
turns.zh: 您帮助建立了印度和世界上一些最成功的市场。我很好奇关于建立一个成功的市场可能有什么教训？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: One thing that I would definitely want to talk about is when you're thinking marketplaces, it's not as a one plus one equals two, it multiplies. We're thinking about three-way marketplaces. You almost not need to think like it's a two-dimensional plane going into three-dimension. It becomes that amount of complexity, and your regular product management and leadership principles start failing. So a bunch of usual suspects will not work. Let me give an example. OKRs will not work. Why not? So, fundamentally, OKRs are a way to think about objectives and key results, but the fundamental assumption here is that it is solving for a kind of user, and that kind of user, you can divide and conquer. Of course, there will be a little bit of tussle between different teams, but you can get them to work with each other. But if it is working for three different kinds of users, then all the goals will all the time be in conflict with each other.
turns.zh: 我肯定想谈论的一件事是，当你思考市场时，它不是一加一等于二，而是乘法。我们正在考虑三向市场。你几乎不需要认为它是一个二维平面进入三维。它变得如此复杂，你的常规产品管理和领导原则开始失败。所以一堆常见的嫌疑人是行不通的。让我举个例子。 OKR 不会起作用。为什么不呢？因此，从根本上来说，OKR 是一种思考目标和关键结果的方法，但这里的基本假设是它正在解决一种用户的问题，而对于这种用户，你可以分而治之。当然，不同团队之间会存在一些争执，但你可以让他们相互合作。但如果它适用于三种不同类型的用户，那么所有目标将始终相互冲突。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are examples of the three users? There's like the delivery person, the restaurant-
turns.zh: 这三个用户的例子是什么？比如送货员、餐厅——

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: The end user. So if you have... I'll give you an example of. On the consumer side, we need to collect more delivery fee. What does that really mean for those other two? On the restaurant side, hey, we need to get more commissions because profitability is a goal. On the delivery partner side, it means pay them less or optimize a little bit more. But once you start moving one lever, those two are already stretched towards the other directions. They're not independent levers in the first place, and the way to even model them out... How will it work? What if we choose X versus what... Ys will change. Y on Z. Z will change. It's almost impossible to do that. (00:59:43): So I've seen OKRs fail multiple times when you're running this kind of a marketplace. Big bets work much better. That's when you say, "Hey, we want to take this bit," but it's all going to be... It's all going to come together as... If we pull this lever, then something else will change. So here's the entire story of, "Let's go make this profitable by making delivery fee higher, but maybe not touching earnings per hour, or maybe not touching restaurant commissions." Things like that. So I've at least found that's a better way to choose strategically which direction we have to go. (01:00:18): The other thing is managing multiple empathies together that's not straightforward. So, again, Swiggy being a real-time, hyper-local marketplace, and we discussed about that, right? As soon as the order comes, what happens between when user does this and when delivery executor is doing something else, and what are absolute different kind of scenarios that are going to be faced by the delivery executor? At the same time, how will I really work with the user to manage their emotions? So you need to manage a whole bunch of these things together, and product management here, you cannot have... The delivery executive product manager only care about that side. They also need to be a champion on the consumer side and vice versa.
turns.zh: 最终用户。所以如果你有......我会给你一个例子。在消费者方面，我们需要收取更多的配送费。这对另外两个人来说到底意味着什么？在餐厅方面，嘿，我们需要获得更多佣金，因为盈利是目标。在交付合作伙伴方面，这意味着少付钱给他们或者多优化一点。但一旦你开始移动一个杠杆，那两个杠杆就已经向其他方向拉伸。首先，它们并不是独立的杠杆，甚至对它们进行建模的方法……它将如何工作？如果我们选择 X 与...Y 会发生变化。 Z 上的 Y。Z 将会改变。这几乎是不可能的。 (00:59:43)：因此，当您运行此类市场时，我多次看到 OKR 失败。大赌注效果更好。那时你会说，“嘿，我们想拿走这一点”，但这一切都会……这一切都会聚集在一起……如果我们拉动这个杠杆，那么其他事情就会改变。所以这就是整个故事，“让我们通过提高送货费来实现盈利，但也许不触及每小时收入，或者也许不触及餐厅佣金。”诸如此类的事情。所以我至少发现这是从战略上选择我们必须走的方向的更好方法。 (01:00:18)：另一件事是同时管理多种同理心，这并不简单。所以，再说一遍，Swiggy 是一个实时、超本地化的市场，我们对此进行了讨论，对吗？一旦订单到来，当用户执行此操作和交付执行者执行其他操作之间会发生什么，以及交付执行者将面临哪些完全不同的场景？同时，我将如何真正与用户一起管理他们的情绪？所以你需要一起管理一大堆这些事情，而这里的产品管理，你不能……交付执行产品经理只关心这一面。他们还需要成为消费者方面的拥护者，反之亦然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I find with marketplaces... Uber went through this, Lyft went through this where the supply often just gets squeezed because they need to deliver for the customer. So drivers end up getting housed. Airbnb hosts get pushed to do things they may not want to do. Imagine delivery people, same thing.
turns.zh: 是的。我发现在市场上……Uber 经历过这个，Lyft 也经历过这个，供应经常受到挤压，因为他们需要为客户送货。所以司机最终都会得到安置。 Airbnb 房东被迫去做他们可能不想做的事情。想象一下送货员，同样的事情。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Now that you mentioned Uber, for example, one of the things that companies which were running taxi businesses. If you have just one limited pool of money, for example, and you want to get the marketplace humming with respect to number of orders per day, how do you decide, "Should I incentivize my users, for example, for the first ride, first 10 rides, and so on, or put zero money in there, but incentivize my drivers?" You need to come here, so you have to think about liquidity also in very different ways, and sometimes you need to pull the lever completely towards the other side. So the experiments also. A/B experiments also don't work, and that's a very unique thing about marketplaces. I mean, not work the way that you would expect them to work because there are network effects all over. So if you have to run A/B experiments on your drivers side, if you put half drivers on A versus half on B, but there is a network effect between the both of them.
turns.zh: 例如，现在您提到了优步，这是经营出租车业务的公司之一。例如，如果你只有一个有限的资金池，并且你想让市场在每天的订单数量方面蓬勃发展，你如何决定，“我应该激励我的用户，例如第一次乘车、前 10 次乘车等等，还是投入零钱，但激励我的司机？”你需要来到这里，所以你必须以非常不同的方式考虑流动性，有时你需要将杠杆完全拉向另一边。故实验也。 A/B 实验也不起作用，这是市场的一个非常独特的事情。我的意思是，不要按照你期望的方式工作，因为到处都有网络效应。因此，如果您必须在驱动程序端运行 A/B 实验，如果您将一半驱动程序放在 A 上，将一半驱动程序放在 B 上，但两者之间存在网络效应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you're trying to decide which side of the marketplace to focus on and prioritize, do you have any lessons or rules of thumb of just focus on the customer and index towards their happiness versus the supply versus, say, the delivery person?
turns.zh: 当您试图决定要关注和优先考虑市场的哪一方面时，您是否有任何经验教训或经验法则可以只关注客户并指数他们的幸福感，而不是供应与送货员？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: There's one thing that I think marketplaces need to realize is that, A, you need to be operating in a stable marketplace. So all sides need to be stable enough so that they're not going to go away. So I think that's a starting point, and that's an important point because once we have established that, then after a stable marketplace, then we say, "Which are the kind of customer that we are in the service for? Which are the customer that we will really focus on?" For example, Amazon is very, very clearly a customer-centric company. If they have to make a choice, they won't because they need to have a stable marketplace. So sellers also are very... as important, but slightly more important than the customer. (01:03:10): For example, if you looked at, say, Taobao or in Alibaba, their way of thinking is their aim in life is to create life-changing experience for 10 million Chinese sellers, and they will create a marketplace from the point of view of sellers which can actually sell. Again, they will have the same consumer app, and a seller work, and so on. They are in the service of sellers, so you really need to derive from the company's vision. I think the way we had thought about it at Swiggy that we had to clarify in our values that the first value is... Initially, it used to be customer comes first, but that was very confusing because everybody is a customer. Even a restaurant is a selling customer and so on. We had to clarify that consumer comes first, the end consumer which is actually eating food because we are a convenience company that delivers to the end consumer, and when you're thinking about restaurants or delivery partners, we work with them because we both are... When you're talking with the delivery partner, Swiggy and the delivery partner, we both are in the service of the customer. So you'll build that app also from that perspective and even the restaurant side also from that perspective that we both are together in the service of the end customer.
turns.zh: 我认为市场需要认识到的一件事是，A，你需要在一个稳定的市场中运营。所以各方都需要足够稳定，这样他们才不会消失。所以我认为这是一个起点，也是一个重要的点，因为一旦我们建立了这一点，那么在稳定的市场之后，我们就会说，“我们为哪些类型的客户提供服务？我们真正关注的客户是哪些？”例如，亚马逊显然是一家以客户为中心的公司。如果他们必须做出选择，他们不会因为他们需要有一个稳定的市场。因此，卖家也非常……同样重要，但比客户稍微重要一点。 (01:03:10): 举个例子，如果你看看淘宝或者阿里巴巴，他们的思维方式是他们的人生目标是为1000万中国卖家创造改变生活的体验，他们会从卖家的角度创建一个真正可以销售的市场。同样，他们将拥有相同的消费者应用程序和卖家工作，等等。他们是为卖家服务的，所以你确实需要从公司的愿景中获得灵感。我认为我们在 Swiggy 的思考方式是，我们必须在我们的价值观中澄清，第一个价值观是……最初，它曾经是客户至上，但这非常令人困惑，因为每个人都是客户。甚至餐馆也是销售顾客等等。我们必须澄清，消费者至上，最终消费者实际上正在吃食物，因为我们是一家向最终消费者提供送货服务的便利公司，当您考虑餐馆或送货合作伙伴时，我们会与他们合作，因为我们都是……当您与送货合作伙伴、Swiggy 和送货合作伙伴交谈时，我们都是在为客户服务。因此，您也将从这个角度构建该应用程序，甚至餐厅方面也将从我们共同为最终客户服务的角度构建该应用程序。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you have probably a hundred more frameworks, and processes, and acronyms we can talk about, but I know you got to go. Is there anything else you wanted to touch on, or is there anything else you want to leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我觉得你可能还有一百多个我们可以讨论的框架、流程和首字母缩略词，但我知道你必须离开。在我们开始激动人心的闪电回合之前，您还有什么想谈的吗？或者您还有什么想留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Just last few words that I want to revise. Work backwards from an amazing future. So first thing is creatively imagine a future, and then work backwards from that, and essentially, think what will make that successful, and be paranoid about... that everything is going to go wrong. Hence, I need to just make sure that it all comes together.
turns.zh: 最后几句话我想修改一下。从美好的未来开始倒退。因此，第一件事就是创造性地想象一个未来，然后从那里开始倒退，本质上，思考什么能让未来成功，并对……一切都会出错感到偏执。因此，我需要确保所有这些都整合在一起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Only the paranoids survive. Great advice to leave people with. We've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 只有偏执狂才能生存。给人们留下的好建议。我们已经进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 您向其他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: One book is Working Backwards. We covered that. The other one that has shaped my beliefs a lot is called How Brands Grow by a professor called Byron Sharp. There are two paths to it, How Brands Grow 1 and 2, that's both very good. The other book which I really love is... and recently, Kunal Shah, who's the founder of Cred, an Indian startup, suggested is The Luxury Strategy. The reason why I love that book is because it gets into the depth of the human psychology behind hierarchies, and how lords, and kings, and those kind of social hierarchies have shaped how people think about aspirational products and so on. So highly recommend it.
turns.zh: 一本书是《逆向工作》。我们对此进行了介绍。另一篇对我的信念影响很大的书是拜伦·夏普（Byron Sharp）教授的《品牌如何成长》（How Brands Grow）。有两条路可以实现，品牌如何成长 1 和 2，都非常好。我真正喜欢的另一本书是……最近，印度初创公司 Cred 的创始人 Kunal Shah 推荐的书是《奢侈品战略》。我喜欢这本书的原因是因为它深入探讨了等级制度背后的人类心理，以及领主、国王和这些社会等级制度如何塑造了人们对理想产品等的看法。所以强烈推荐它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 您最近最喜欢的电影或电视节目是什么？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: I really like to do reruns of The Office. I was trying to think about this as, "What is a recent movie that I watched?" I'm like, "No." I keep on going back to The Office and some other episode. Like today, I have a lot of stories from Michael Scott.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢重播《办公室》。我试着思考这个问题：“我最近看的一部电影是什么？”我说：“不。”我不断地回到《办公室》和其他一些剧集。就像今天一样，我有很多迈克尔·斯科特的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. The US one, not the British one, or do you watch both?
turns.zh: 好的。美国的，不是英国的，还是两者都看？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: No. I watch both, but the US one has a lot more seasons.
turns.zh: 不。我两部都看，但美国的有更多季。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates when you're interviewing product-manager-specific?
turns.zh: 当你面试产品经理时，你有最喜欢问候选人的面试问题吗？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: "Which are the products where you decide speed is more important versus which are the products where you have to say excellence is what's important?" I think that gives me a good understanding of their frameworks and why they're just saying what, and then we go back into concrete examples where they chose one versus the other, and then take it from there.
turns.zh: “您认为哪些产品的速度更重要，而哪些产品您必须说卓越更重要？”我认为这让我很好地理解了他们的框架以及为什么他们只是说了什么，然后我们回到具体的例子，他们选择了一个而不是另一个，然后从那里开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then, what do you look for In a good answer to that question?
turns.zh: 那么，您在寻找该问题的良好答案时需要什么？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: I look for, essentially, their assessment of risk, their assessment of how important or how well have they assessed the market and the competition or the competitive products in that market. If their answer is, "Let's ship something, and we'll find out, and so on," that also gives me, basically, a point of view that they really don't understand that this product, what they're talking about with the shipping speed, is not really... The V part of the MVP is not viable or is not... I don't know. How do you call the MLP or whatever? But it's not differentiated enough that it can be marketed. It is not worth enough where we can take it to user. It's not going to work for a lazy win and selfish user, and maybe that's not the answer towards speed versus excellence versus, for example, there's some products which are... There's a very clear competitive differentiation that we can find. There was a clear market gap. I want to launch something even if it is half-baked. No problem. I want to go, take it out, get user feedback, I trade, and so on. So understanding of the market, A, but B, also understanding of the core orientation.
turns.zh: 本质上，我寻找的是他们对风险的评估，他们对市场以及该市场中的竞争或竞争产品的重要性或评估程度的评估。如果他们的答案是，“让我们发货一些东西，我们会找到答案，等等”，这基本上也给了我一个观点，即他们真的不明白这个产品，他们所说的发货速度，并不是真的...... MVP 的 V 部分不可行或不...... 我不知道。你怎么称呼 MLP 之类的？但它的差异化程度还不够，无法推向市场。如果我们可以把它带给用户的话，它的价值还不够。它不会为懒惰的胜利和自私的用户工作，也许这不是速度与卓越的答案，例如，有一些产品......我们可以找到非常明显的竞争差异化。存在明显的市场缺口。我想推出一些东西，即使它是半生不熟的。没问题。我想去，把它拿出来，获取用户反馈，我进行交易，等等。所以了解市场，A，但B，也了解核心定位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It comes back to your ongoing advice of being full-stack in a lot of ways, and in this case, being a full-stack PM thinking about marketing, launch, and adoption, all those things. Next question, what is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 这又回到了你一直以来关于在很多方面成为全栈的建议，在这种情况下，作为一个全栈 PM 思考营销、发布和采用，所有这些事情。下一个问题，您最近发现的您真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: The very recent product that I like is called RISE. It's a sleep track app because I am half insomniac, and for the longest time, I was thinking about, "How can I track this? What am I doing, and how can I actually get better at this?" So I really like the way that they actually help the end user. It's just been a week since I've started using it, but recommend it.
turns.zh: 我最近喜欢的产品叫做 RISE。这是一个睡眠跟踪应用程序，因为我半失眠症，在很长一段时间里，我都在想，“我怎样才能跟踪这个？我在做什么，我怎样才能真正做得更好？”所以我真的很喜欢他们实际帮助最终用户的方式。虽然刚开始使用一周，但还是推荐一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Has that helped your sleep yet or too soon to say?
turns.zh: 这对您的睡眠有帮助吗？还是现在说还为时过早？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: It's helped me track my sleep, so it's... Now, it's getting into the zone where it is actionable, but I like it.
turns.zh: 它帮助我跟踪我的睡眠，所以它......现在，它正在进入可操作的区域，但我喜欢它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, okay. We'll see.
turns.zh: 好吧，好吧。我们拭目以待。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: We'll see.
turns.zh: 我们拭目以待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, share with people, think about in either work or life?
turns.zh: 您是否有一条最喜欢的人生格言，是您在工作或生活中经常回顾、与人分享、思考的？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: I would call it a life motto as much, but one of the things that I keep telling my people who work with me, alongside me, and so on is, "Stop externalizing." That's one, which also means the more artistic way to say that is you are the reason for your own misery. So that's something that I keep using a lot more in a fun way. But if things go wrong, if that leadership meeting didn't happen in that way, if my product bombed, and so on, go back and let's ask ourselves what could we have done better, what I could have done better, and so on. Of course, because I'm also a poker player, so in a way, I understand there is half luck involved and half skill. But over a long period of time, if it's only luck and you're failing, and failing, and failing, you have to go and look back at your skill. So, yeah. You are the reason for your own misery.
turns.zh: 我也将其称为人生座右铭，但我不断告诉与我一起工作、与我并肩工作的人的一件事是，“停止外在化”。这就是其中之一，这也意味着用更艺术的方式来说，你是自己痛苦的原因。所以我一直以一种有趣的方式更多地使用它。但如果出现问题，如果领导会议没有以这种方式举行，如果我的产品失败了，等等，那么我们就回去问问自己，哪些方面我们可以做得更好，哪些方面我可以做得更好，等等。当然，因为我也是一名扑克玩家，所以在某种程度上，我明白这其中一半是运气，一半是技巧。但在很长一段时间内，如果只是运气，而你不断失败，不断失败，你就必须回头审视自己的技能。所以，是的。你就是你自己痛苦的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. Be very empowering, and be responsible. Final question. I was stalking your LinkedIn. You host an event called The Secret Soiree, which is not that secret because you post about it, but I'm curious, just what is that all about, and what got you to do these sorts of events?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个建议。非常有权力，并且有责任感。最后一个问题。我在跟踪你的 LinkedIn。你举办了一个名为“秘密晚会”的活动，这并不是那么秘密，因为你发布了有关它的信息，但我很好奇，这到底是关于什么的，是什么让你去做这些类型的活动？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: So we just started, me and an ex-colleague of mine, Shivangi. So we essentially wanted to meet cool people around. So that's how it started. Interesting people without agenda who can come together and discuss interesting stuff about entrepreneurship, about startups, about products, about connections, and so on, and so forth. So it just started like that, and now we are onto many, many more interesting things that we are bringing in terms of cohorts which will be team-based. So it could be around product management, around marketing, around growth, and so on. We are strictly keeping it not-for-profit for at least the next year, but long way to go.
turns.zh: 所以我们才刚刚开始，我和我的前同事 Shivangi。所以我们本质上是想认识周围很酷的人。事情就是这样开始的。没有议程的有趣的人可以聚集在一起讨论有关创业、初创公司、产品、联系等等的有趣内容。所以事情就这样开始了，现在我们正在做很多很多更有趣的事情，我们将在基于团队的群体方面带来更多有趣的事情。所以它可以围绕产品管理、营销、增长等等。我们至少在明年严格将其保持为非营利性质，但还有很长的路要走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing, and so for listeners, is this something they could join? Who should look into this? Who is this for?
turns.zh: 太棒了，那么对于听众来说，这是他们可以加入的吗？谁应该调查这个问题？这是给谁的？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Absolutely. At that time, probably, we'll not call it The Secret Soiree once we have probably expanded.
turns.zh: 绝对地。到那时，一旦我们可能扩大规模，我们可能就不会再将其称为“秘密晚会”了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No longer secret. Okay. Cool, and then I guess they just follow you on LinkedIn, right? That's how they can keep up to date with these sorts of events. Okay. Cool.
turns.zh: 不再是秘密。好的。酷，然后我猜他们只是在 LinkedIn 上关注你，对吗？这就是他们能够及时了解此类事件的方式。好的。凉爽的。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yes, on LinkedIn as well as on Twitter.
turns.zh: 是的，在 LinkedIn 和 Twitter 上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Anuj, we've gone through so many topics. We've talked about breaking bad and full-stack product management, full-stack thinking, working backwards, bread and butter, rule of threes. I don't know. So many things. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and follow up on anything we've talked about, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 惊人的。 Anuj，我们讨论了很多话题。我们讨论了破局和全栈产品管理、全栈思维、逆向工作、面包和黄油、三人法则。我不知道。这么多的事情。最后两个问题。如果人们想要联系并跟进我们谈论的任何事情，可以在哪里找到您？听众如何对您有用？

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Yes. So I'm on Twitter, so on twitter.com/anujrathi, and LinkedIn, you can just search my name. I'm pretty active on both of them. I do a bunch of... not podcasts all the time like you host, Lenny, but a bunch of other events as well as talks, so. I keep on posting on Twitter. They can find me there.
turns.zh: 是的。我在 Twitter、twitter.com/anujrathi 和 LinkedIn 上，你可以搜索我的名字。我对这两件事都非常积极。我做了很多……不是像你主持的那样一直播客，莱尼，而是很多其他活动以及演讲，所以。我继续在推特上发帖。他们可以在那里找到我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Anuj, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 惊人的。阿努吉，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Anuj Rathi
turns.en: Thank you so much, Lenny, for hosting.
turns.zh: 非常感谢莱尼的主持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my pleasure. Bye, everyone. (01:12:05): Thank you so much for listening. If you found this valuable, you can subscribe to the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. Also, please consider giving us a rating or leaving a review as that really helps other listeners find the podcast. You can find all past episodes or learn more about the show at lennyspodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 这是我的荣幸。再见，大家。 (01:12:05)：非常感谢您的收听。如果您发现这很有价值，您可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或您最喜欢的播客应用程序上订阅该节目。另外，请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，因为这确实有助于其他听众找到播客。您可以在 lennyspodcast.com 上找到所有过去的剧集或了解有关该节目的更多信息。下一集见。
